Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 34, verse 1:

Surat Saba' is Meccan according to all scholars, except for one verse concerning which there is disagreement, and it is His Exalted saying: ﴿And those who have been given knowledge see﴾ and so on. One group said: it is Meccan, and what is meant by the believers are the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ; this was said by Ibn 'Abbas. Another group said: it is Medinan, and what is meant by the believers are those who embraced Islam in Medina, such as 'Abdullah ibn Salam and others; this was said by Muqatil. Qatadah said: they are the community of Muhammad ﷺ, the believers in him, whoever they may be. It has fifty-four verses.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Praise be to Allah, to whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, and to Him belongs praise in the Hereafter. And He is the All-Wise, the All-Aware.﴾ (1)

(﴿Praise be to Allah, to whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾) The word "alladhi" (who/which) is in a position of genitive as an adjective (na't) or an apposition (badal). It may also be in a position of nominative by implying a subject (mubtada' muqaddar), and in a position of accusative with the meaning of "I mean." Sibawayh related "al-hamdu lillahi ahlu al-hamd" with nominative, accusative and genitive. Complete praise and all-encompassing commendation belong entirely to Allah, since all blessings come from Him. The discussion of this has already passed at the beginning of al-Fatihah [see vol. 1, p. 131].

(And to Him belongs praise in the Hereafter) It was said: this refers to His Exalted saying: ﴿And they will say, "Praise be to Allah, who has fulfilled His promise to us"﴾ [see vol. 15, p. 284 onward] [az-Zumar: 74]. And it was said: it refers to His saying: ﴿And the last of their prayer will be, "Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds"﴾ [see vol. 8, p. 313] [Yunus: 10]. So He is praised in the Hereafter just as He is praised in this world, and He is the Owner of the Hereafter just as He is the Owner of the first life.

(And He is the All-Wise) in His actions.

(The All-Aware) regarding the affairs of His creation.

Al-Qurtubi's commentary on Surah 34, verse 2:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He knows what enters into the earth﴾, meaning what goes into it of rain and other things, as He said: ﴿then He makes it into springs in the earth﴾ [Az-Zumar: 21], of treasures, hidden wealth, the dead, and that which is a *kifat* for them [[Al-kifat: the place into which a thing is gathered and held.]].

﴿And what comes out of it﴾ of plants and other things.

﴿And what descends from the sky﴾ of rains, snow, hail, thunderbolts, provisions, decrees, and blessings. ʿAli ibn Abi Talib recited "wa-ma nunazzilu" with the nun and with shaddah.

﴿And what ascends into it﴾ of angels and the deeds of the servants. This was said by al-Hasan and others. ﴿And He is the Most Merciful, the Most Forgiving﴾.

[[See vol. 15, p. 245.]]

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 34, verses 3–4:**

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And those who disbelieve say, "The Hour will not come upon us."﴾ It was said: the intended people are the people of Makkah. Muqatil said: Abu Sufyan said to the disbelievers of Makkah, "By al-Lat and al-'Uzza, the Hour will never come upon us, and we will never be resurrected." So Allah said: "Say," O Muhammad, "Yes, by my Lord, it will surely come upon you." Harun narrated from Talq al-Mu'allim, who said: "I heard our shaykhs reading 'Say, yes, by my Lord, it will surely come to you' with the ya' (لَيَأْتِيَنَّكُمْ), they took it according to the meaning, as if he had said: 'the Resurrection will surely come to you, or its command,' as in His saying: ﴿Do they wait for anything except that the angels come to them, or that the command of your Lord comes?﴾ [Al-An'am: 158]. See vol. 10, p. 102.

These disbelievers acknowledge the origination (al-ibtida') but deny the restoration (al-i'adah). This is a contradiction, since they have admitted the power to resurrect, yet they say, "Even if He is able, He will not do it." This is arbitrary judgment, after the report was conveyed through the tongues of the Messengers that He will resurrect creation. When a report comes about something that is possible in act and within power, denying the one whose truthfulness is obligatory is impossible.

(ʿĀlimu al-ghayb) with the nominative (bi-al-raf') is the recitation of Nafi' and Ibn Kathir, as a beginning (ibtida'), and its predicate is (lā yaʿzubu ʿanhu, "nothing escapes from Him"). 'Asim and Abu 'Amr read ʿālimi with the genitive (bi-al-khafd), meaning "Praise belongs to Allah, the Knower," so on this reading it is not good to stop at His saying "la-ta'tiyannakum." Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read ʿallāmi al-ghayb as an intensive form (al-mubalaghah) and as a qualifier (al-na't).

(Lā yaʿzubu ʿanhu) means: does not go absent from Him. It is also read yaʿzibu. Al-Farra' said: "The kasr (yaʿzibu) is more beloved to me." Al-Nahhas said: it is the recitation of Yahya ibn Wathhab, and it is a well-known dialect. One says: 'azaba yaʿzubu and yaʿzibu when he went far away and was absent.

(Mithqala dharrah) means: the amount of a small ant.

(Fi al-samawati wa la fi al-ardi wa la asghara min dhalika wa la akbar): in the recitation of al-A'mash, "wa la asghara min dhalika wa la akbar" is in the accusative in both, as coordinated (ʿatfan) upon "dharrah." The common recitation has the nominative, as coordinated upon "mithqal."

(Illa fi kitabin mubin) means: He is the Knower of what He created, and nothing is hidden from Him.

(Liyajziya) is in the subjunctive by the lam of purpose (lam kay), and the implied meaning is: "they will surely come to you, so that He may recompense."

(Alladhina amanu wa 'amilu al-salihat) with reward, and the disbelievers with punishment.

(Ulaʾika) means: the believers.

(Lahum maghfiratun) for their sins.

(Wa rizqun karim) and this is Paradise.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 34, verse 5:

Allah's words: ﴿And those who strive against Our signs﴾ means: who work to nullify Our proofs and deny Our signs.

(Mu'ajizin) means: competing, thinking that they can outdo Us, and that Allah is not able to resurrect them in the Hereafter, and they thought that We would leave them unpunished. "For these there is a painful punishment of a kind of wrath (rijz)." It is said: 'aajazahu and a'jazahu, meaning he overcame him and outpaced him. "Painful" (alim) is the reading of Nafi' with a kasra, as an adjective of "rijz," since rijz is punishment. Allah says: ﴿So We sent down upon those who did wrong a punishment (rijz) from the sky﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 59].[[See vol. 1, p. 415 and following.]] Ibn Kathir and Hafs, from 'Asim, read "azabun min rijzin alim" with a damma on the "meem" here and in "al-Jathiyah,"[[See vol. 16, p. 159 and following.]] as an adjective of "adhab" (punishment). Ibn Kathir, Ibn Muhaysin, Humayd ibn Qays, Mujahid and Abu 'Amr read "mu'ajjizin," meaning discouraging, i.e., they discouraged people from believing in the miracles and the signs of the Qur'an.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 34, verse 6:

When He mentioned those who strove to nullify prophethood, He clarified that those who were given knowledge see that the Qur'an is the truth. Muqatil said: "Those who were given knowledge" are the believers among the People of the Book. Ibn 'Abbas said: they are the Companions of Muhammad (ﷺ). It was also said: all Muslims, and this is the most sound view because of its generality. The "seeing" (ru'yah) here means knowing ('ilm), and it is in a place of nasb (accusative) by coordination with "li-yajziya," meaning: so that He may recompense, and so that He may see. This was said by al-Zajjaj and al-Farra'. But this is open to question, because His saying "li-yajziya" is connected to His saying "la-ta'tiyannakum" (the Hour will surely come to you), and one does not say: "The Hour will surely come to you so that those who were given knowledge may see that the Qur'an is the truth," for they see the Qur'an as the truth even if the Hour does not come to them. The correct view is that it is in the nominative (raf') by way of resumption (isti'naf), as mentioned by al-Qushayri. I say: and when "li-yajziya" is connected in meaning to "uthbita dhalika fi kitabin mubin" (that was recorded in a clear Book), it is good to coordinate "wa-yara" with it, meaning: and He also recorded, so that those who were given knowledge may see that the Qur'an is the truth. [In the originals: "and He also recorded the seeing of those who were given knowledge".] It is also permissible that it be a new sentence (musta'naf). "Alladhi" is in the place of nasb as the first object of "yara," "huwa al-haqq" is the second object, and "huwa" is a separator (fasilah). The Kufans say "huwa" is an 'imad (supporting pronoun). It is also permissible to read it in the nominative as the subject (mubtada'), with "al-haqq" as its predicate, and the clause is in the place of nasb as the second object. The accusative is more common where the definite article is present according to all grammarians, and likewise where the predicate is indefinite and does not take the definite article, so that it resembles the definite. If the predicate is a known noun, as in your saying: "kana akhuka huwa Zayd," al-Farra' holds that the preferred choice in it is the nominative. Likewise: "kana Muhammad huwa 'Amr." The reason for his preferring the nominative is that where there is no definite article, it resembles the indefinite, as in your saying: "kana Zayd huwa jalis," because in this case only the nominative is permissible.

(And He guides to the path of the Mighty, the Praiseworthy) That is: the Qur'an guides to the way of Islam, which is the religion of Allah. By His saying "al-'Aziz" (the Mighty) it indicates that He cannot be overcome, and by His saying "al-Hamid" (the Praiseworthy) it indicates that the attribute of incapacity is not befitting to Him.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 34, verse 7:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And those who disbelieve say, "Shall we direct you to a man who will inform you"﴾. The lam may be assimilated into the nun (idgham) if you wish, due to their proximity to each other.

"Will inform you when you are completely torn apart" (yunabbi'ukum idha muzziqtum kulla mumazzaq). This is a report about those who said: ﴿The Hour will not come upon us﴾ [Saba': 3]. That is, "Shall we guide you to a man who will inform you," meaning, who will say to you: "You will be resurrected after decay in the graves." This came from the extremity of their denial.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was well known and a prominent figure among the Quraysh, and his announcement of the Resurrection was widespread among them. So what is the meaning of their saying, 'Shall we direct you to a man who will inform you,' where they made him indefinite for them and offered to direct them to him, as one is directed to an unknown person concerning an unknown matter?" I say: They intended by this mockery, derision and ridicule (al-tanz wa'l-huzu wa'l-sukhriyya), and they put it in the form of riddling (al-tahakki) with some of the riddles by which people pose questions for laughter and amusement, feigning ignorance of him and of his matter."

"Idha" is in the position of a accusative (nasb), and its governing element is "muzziqtum," as stated by al-Nahhas. It is not permissible for its governing element to be "yunabbi'ukum," because he does not inform them at that time. Nor is it permissible for its governing element to be what follows "inna," because that does not govern what precedes it, and what follows it, nor its complement, may not precede it. Al-Zajjaj permitted that its governing element be an omitted word, the estimate being: "When you are torn apart, every tearing, you will be resurrected," or "he informs you that you will be resurrected when you are torn apart."

Al-Mahdawi said: "Muzziqtum" does not govern it, because it is a complement of an annexed noun (mudaf ilayhi), and the annexed noun does not govern the noun to which it is annexed. Some permitted it, by making "idha" conditional (lil-mujazat), in which case what follows it governs it, since it is not annexed to anything. "Idha" in the conditional sense occurs most often in poetry.

The meaning of "muzziqtum kulla mumazzaq" is: you will be scattered in every kind of scattering. Al-Mazq is the tearing of things; it is said: a garment that is torn (thawb mazeeq), and mamzuq, mutamazziq, and mumazzaq.

The Almighty's words, **﴿Has he invented a lie against God, or is there madness in him?﴾**: When the interrogative alif (*alif al-istifham*) was prefixed, the connecting alif (*alif al-wasl*) was dispensed with and dropped. The opening of the interrogative alif was vowelled with a fatha to distinguish it from the connecting alif. This has already been discussed fully in the surah of Maryam at the Almighty's words, **﴿Has he looked into the unseen?﴾** [Maryam: 78] [See vol. 11, p. 147].

**(Or is there madness in him?)** This is linked to what preceded it from the words of the polytheists. The meaning is: the polytheists said, "Has he invented a lie against God?" *Iftira'* (fabrication) means *ikhtilaq* (making up). **"Or is there madness in him?"** means *junun* (insanity), meaning that he speaks what he does not know. Then He answered them, saying: **(Nay, but those who do not believe in the Hereafter are in the torment and far error)**. That is, the matter is not as they said. Rather, he is the most truthful of the truthful. Whoever denies the Resurrection will be in torment tomorrow and in error from the right path today, since they have come to disable God and to attribute fabrication to one whom God has supported with miracles.

Al-Qurtubi, in his commentary (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran), on surah 34, verse 9:

Allah, exalted is He, informed that the One who was able to create the heavens and the earth and what is between them is able to resurrect (them) and to hasten punishment upon them. So He cited His power over them, and that the heavens and the earth are His dominion, and that they encompass them from every side. "So how can they feel secure from the earth swallowing them up (khasf) or a piece of the sky falling upon them (kisf), as was done to Qarun and the companions of al-Aykah?"

Hamzah and al-Kisa'i recited "in yasha' yakhsif bihimu al-ardh aw yusqit" with the ya' in all three (verbs), meaning: if Allah wills, He commands the earth so that it swallows them up, or the sky so that it drops pieces (kisafan) upon them. The rest recited with the nun, out of glorification (of Allah). As-Sulami and Hafs recited "kisafan" with a fatha on the sin. The rest recited it with sukun. Its explanation has already been given under "Subhan" [[see vol. 10, p. (330)]] and elsewhere.

(Indeed in that there is surely a sign) meaning: in what we have mentioned of Our power, "a sign" meaning a clear proof.

(For every servant who turns back in repentance) meaning: one who repents and returns to Allah with his heart. The one who turns back (munib) is singled out for mention because he is the one who benefits from reflecting upon the proofs and signs of Allah.

(And We certainly gave David a favour from Us.) This shows those who deny the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ) that sending messengers is not a novel matter. Rather, We sent messengers and supported them with miracles, and We brought punishment upon those who opposed them. "Ātaynā" means "We gave." "Faḍlan" means a matter by which We favoured him over others. Scholars differ on what this favour was, and there are nine opinions:

The first is prophethood. The second is the Zabur (the Psalms). The third is knowledge, as Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And We certainly gave David and Solomon knowledge﴾ [[See vol. 13, p. 163 onwards.]] [an-Naml: 15]. The fourth is strength, as Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And remember Our servant David, the possessor of strength﴾ [[See vol. 15, p. 158.]] [Ṣād: 17]. The fifth is the subjugation of the mountains and the people, as Allah the Exalted says: "O mountains, echo the praises along with him" [[See vol. 15, p. 184.]]. The sixth is repentance, as Allah the Exalted says: "So We forgave him that" [[See vol. 15, p. 188.]] [Ṣād: 25]. The seventh is judging with justice, as Allah the Exalted says: "O David, We have made you a khalīfah (vicegerent) on the earth" [Ṣād: 26], and the verse continues [[See vol. 15, p. 159.]]. The eighth is the softening of iron, as He the Exalted says: "And We softened for him the iron" [[See vol. 15, p. 159.]]. The ninth is beauty of voice. David, peace be upon him, had a beautiful voice and a beautiful face. Beauty of voice is a gift from Allah the Exalted and a bounty from Him, and this is what is meant by His saying, blessed and exalted is He: ﴿He adds to creation what He wills﴾ [[See from p. 318 onwards in this part.]] [Fāṭir: 1], as will come, Allah willing.

The Prophet (ﷺ) said to Abū Mūsā: "You have indeed been given one of the mizmārs of the family of David." The scholars said: al-mizmār and al-mazmūr mean a beautiful voice, and the wind instrument (mizmār) was named after it. Many jurists of the cities have deemed recitation with embellishment and melodic modulation (tarjīʿ) to be good. This has already passed in the introduction to this book [[See vol. 1, p. 11 onwards.]], and all praise is due to Allah.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿O mountains, echo the praises along with him﴾, means: And We said, "O mountains, echo along with him," that is, glorify (sabbiḥī) along with him, because He, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, We subjected the mountains to glorify with him, in the evening and at sunrise﴾ [[See vol. 15, p. 159.]] [Ṣād: 18]. Abū Maysara said: it is glorification in the language of Abyssinia. The meaning of the glorification of the mountains is that Allah the Exalted created glorification in them, just as He created speech in the tree, so that what is heard from them is what is heard from one who glorifies, as a miracle for David, upon him be prayer and peace. It was also said: the meaning is "travel with him wherever he wishes," from ta'wīb, which is travelling the whole day and descending at night. Ibn Muqbil said:

"We joined a tribe that had travelled on [at the time of] return, after we had pushed back the sun's rays, while the gaze was inclining."

Al-Ḥasan, Qatādah and others recited "awwibī maʿahu," meaning "return with him," from āba ya'ūbu, when one returns: awban, awbatan and iyāban. It was also said: the meaning is "move with him in the manner in which David moves during the day." Thus, when he recited the Zabur, the mountains resonated with him and the birds listened to him, as though they were doing what he did. Wahb ibn Munabbih said: the meaning is "lament with him," and the birds assisted him in that. When he called out in lamentation, the mountains answered him with their echo, and the birds gathered above him. So the echo of the mountains that people hear has been from that day until this hour. He was thus supported by the mountains and the birds so that he would not experience a lapse [[Al-fatra: weakness.]]. When a lapse came upon him, he was stirred, that is, he rose and moved, and was strengthened by the support of the mountains and the birds. He had been given a voice such that wild beasts crowded from the mountains because of its beauty, and flowing water would stop flowing, standing still for his voice.

"Wa-l-ṭayr" (and the birds) in the nominative is the reading of Ibn Abī Isḥāq, Naṣr (on the authority of ʿĀṣim), Ibn Harmuz and Maslamah ibn ʿAbd al-Malik, taken as a conjunction with the wording "al-jibāl" or with the pronoun in "awwibī," and the intervening word "maʿahu" makes it acceptable. The rest read it in the accusative, as a conjunction with the position of "yā jibāl" (meaning: We called the mountains and the birds), as Sībawayh said. According to Abū ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ, it is in the accusative by supplying a verb with the meaning "and We subjected the birds to him." Al-Kisāʾī said: it is conjoined, meaning "and We gave him the birds," taking it as parallel to "And We certainly gave David a favour." Al-Naḥḥās said: it may also be a maf'ūl maʿahu (object of accompaniment), as you say: "the water levelled with the wood." I heard al-Zajjāj permitting: "I stood with Zayd," so the meaning is "return with him and with the birds."

(And We softened for him the iron.) Ibn ʿAbbās said: it became to him like wax. Al-Ḥasan said: like dough; he would work it without fire. Al-Suddī said: the iron in his hand was like wet clay, dough and wax; he would shape it as he wished, without putting it in fire or striking it with a hammer. Muqātil said the same. He would finish a coat of mail in part of a day or part of a night, and its price was a thousand dirhams. It was also said: he was given a strength by which he could bend iron. The reason for this was that when David, peace be upon him, became ruler over the Children of Israel, he met an angel, and David thought he was a human; David was in disguise, going out in secret to ask about himself and his conduct among the Children of Israel. David said to that person who had appeared to him: "What do you say about this king, David?" The angel said to him: "An excellent servant, were it not for a flaw in him." David said: "And what is it?" He said: "He takes his provision from the public treasury. If he ate from the work of his own hands, his virtues would be complete." So David returned, and called upon Allah to teach him a craft and make it easy for him. So He taught him the craft of making chain mail (labūs), as Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said in Sūrat al-Anbiyāʾ [[See vol. 11, p. 320.]]. He softened the iron for him, and he made coats of mail. He would make a coat of mail in the span between his day and night, which was worth a thousand dirhams, until he saved much of it, and his household's livelihood became comfortable. He gave charity to the poor and the needy, and he spent a third of his wealth on the public interests of the Muslims. He was the first to make coats of mail and fashion them, whereas before that they had been plates. It is said that he would sell each coat for four thousand. The word "dir" (coat of mail) is feminine when it is for war, while "dir" of a woman (a woman's shift) is masculine.

Issue: In this verse there is evidence that people of virtue learn crafts, and that practising them does not diminish their rank; rather, it adds to their excellence and virtues, since they gain humility in themselves and independence from others, and earning lawful income free from obligation to others. In the Ṣaḥīḥ, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The best food a man eats is from the work of his own hand, and the Prophet of Allah, David, used to eat from the work of his own hand." This has already passed in Sūrat al-Anbiyāʾ, and all praise is due to Allah.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 34, verse 11:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Make full coats of mail﴾, meaning full coats of mail, that is, complete, perfect and wide ones. It is said: "sabagha" the coat of mail, the garment and other things, when it covers everything that is on it and extends beyond it.

(And measure well in the links.) Qatadah said: The coats of mail before him were plates, so they were heavy. Therefore he was commanded to apply measure to what combines lightness and strength, that is, measure what you take from these two meanings in its proper proportion: do not aim at strength so that it becomes heavy, nor at lightness so that it removes protection. Ibn Zayd said: The measure he was commanded to observe concerns the size of the ring, that is, do not make them small so that they are weak and the coats of mail cannot withstand blows, nor make them large so that the wearer is reached. Ibn Abbas said: The measure he was commanded to observe concerns the rivet, that is, do not make the rivet of the coat of mail thin so that it wobbles [[al-qalaq: that it does not settle in one place.]], nor thick so that it breaks the rings. It is narrated as "yaqsimu" with the qaf, and the fa' is also a narration. "In the links": al-sard is the weaving of the rings of coats of mail, and from it the maker of coat-of-mail rings is called al-sarrad and al-zarrad, the zay replacing the sin, as it is said: sarrat and zarrat. Al-sard also means stitching; it is said: "sarada yasrudu" when he stitched. Al-misrad is the awl, and it is also called sarrad. Al-Shammakh said: "Our horsemen then followed in succession into your houses, as the hard-hooved ones follow the sard of the reins."

Al-sirad is the thong with which something is stitched. Labid said: "He fastens its plates with the horn, obliquely, as the thong comes out of the worn shoe."

It is said: "He sarada the speech and the fast", so al-sard in both means to bring them one after another in a single sequence, and from it comes sard al-kalam (the continuity of speech). In the hadith of Aisha: The Prophet (ﷺ) did not speak continuously as you do; he would relate a narration which, if one counting wished to count it, he could enumerate. Sibawayh said: From it comes "rajul sarandā", meaning bold, [[that is, he does not waver or bend; this is applied to both male and female.]] because he advances against people. The origin of this lies in the stitching of the coat of mail, which means to make it firm and to make the arrangement of its rings continuous and uniform. Labid said:

He made the iron into double coats, its links woven, to attain long life without being overcome.

Abu Dhu'ayb said:

And upon them two coats woven, which Dawud completed or the artisan of full coats, Tubba', [[qada: completed them or finished them. Al-sun' (with vowel): skill in work. Here al-sun' is Tubba', a king of the kings of Himyar. It is also narrated as "aw sun' al-sawabigh".]]

(And do righteous deeds.) That is, a righteous deed. This is addressed to Dawud and his family, as He said: ﴿Work, O family of Dawud, in gratitude﴾ [Saba': 13].

(Indeed, I am Seeing of what you do.)

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 34, verse 12:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And to Solomon [We subjected] the wind﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: the implied meaning is "and We subjected the wind to Solomon." ʿĀṣim, in the transmission of Abu Bakr from him, read "al-rīḥu" (the wind) in the nominative (raf'), on the basis of the inchoative (ibtida'), and the meaning is "for him is the subjection of the wind," or on the basis of settledness (istiqrar), meaning "and for Solomon the wind is settled (thabitatan)," and in this reading is that first meaning. If someone says: when you say "I gave Zayd a dirham and for ʿAmr is a dinar," with the nominative, the first meaning is absent, and it is possible that you did not give him the dinar. It has been said: the matter is as stated, but the verse, in terms of meaning, is contrary to this, because it is known that no one subjected it except Allah, mighty and majestic.

(Its morning journey is a month, and its evening journey is a month) meaning the distance of a month's travel. Al-Hasan said: he would set out in the morning from Damascus and take his midday rest at Istakhr, and between them is a month's journey for a swift traveller; then he would set out in the evening from Istakhr and spend the night at Kabul, and between them is a month for a swift traveller. Al-Suddi said: it would carry him in one day the distance of two months. Saʿid ibn Jubayr transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: when Solomon sat, four hundred thousand chairs were set up around him. The chiefs of mankind sat nearest to him, the common people of mankind sat next to them, the chiefs of the jinn sat next to the common people of mankind, and the common jinn sat next to them. Over each chair was appointed a bird for a task that it knew. Then the wind would lift them, and the birds would shade them from the sun. He would set out in the morning from Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem) to Istakhr, and spend the night at Bayt al-Maqdis. Then Ibn ʿAbbas recited: "Its morning journey is a month, and its evening journey is a month." Wahb ibn Munabbih said: it was mentioned to me that a dwelling by the side of the Tigris had written on it, by one of Solomon's companions, whether from the jinn or from mankind: "We alighted and did not build it, and we found it built. Our morning journey was from Istakhr, and we shortened it. And we will set out from it, if Allah, exalted, wills, and we shall spend the night in al-Sham (Syria)." Al-Hasan said: horses occupied Solomon until the ʿAsr prayer had passed him by, so he slaughtered the horses, and Allah replaced them for him with something better and swifter: the wind, which runs by His command wherever He wills, its morning journey a month and its evening journey a month. Ibn Zayd said: Solomon's residence was in the city of Tadmur, and he had commanded the devils, before his departure from al-Sham to Iraq, and they built it for him with flat stones (al-ṣuffāḥ) [[al-Ṣuffāḥ (Karmān): broad, thin stones.]], pillars, and white and yellow marble. And concerning it al-Nabigha said:

*Except Solomon, when the Deity said to him: "Stand over the wilderness and restrain it from error (al-fanad) [[al-Ḥadd: prevention. al-Fanad: error.]],*

*And tame the jinn (khayyis) [[Khayyis: subdue.]]; indeed I have permitted them to build Tadmur with flat stones and pillars.*

*Whoever obeys you, benefit him by his obedience, as he obeyed you, and guide him to right conduct.*

*And whoever disobeys you, punish him with a punishment that deters the wrongdoer, and do not dwell upon resentment (ḍamad) [[al-Ḍamad: rancour.]].*

These verses were found engraved on a rock in the land of Yashkur. One of Solomon's companions, peace be upon him, composed them:

*We, and there is no power except the power of our Lord, return to our homelands from the land of Tadmur.*

*When we return, the time of our return is a month's journey, and the morning journey is for another.*

*People who sold their souls to Allah willingly, for the victory of the son of Dawud, the pure prophet.*

*For them is virtue and elevation in the lofty matters of the religion, and if they are ever ascribed to a lineage, it is to the best of groups.*

*When they ride the obedient wind, it hastens, outstripping its month, falling short of nothing.*

*Birds in ranks shade them; whenever they flutter above them, they are not startled.*

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We caused a fount of copper to flow for him﴾. al-Qitr is copper (al-nuḥās), according to Ibn ʿAbbas and others. It flowed for him a distance of three days, as water flows, and it was in the land of Yemen. It is reported that copper had not melted for anyone before him, and it used not to melt; from his time it melted. Today people benefit only from what Allah, exalted, brought forth for Solomon. Qatadah said: Allah caused a spring to flow which he used for whatever he wished. It was asked of ʿIkrimah: "To where did it flow?" He said: "I do not know!" Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, and al-Suddi said: a spring of brass (ṣuf) flowed for him for three days and their nights. al-Qushayri said: the restriction of the flowing to three days has no known limit, and perhaps it is an error of the transmitter, for in a report from Mujahid that it flowed from San'a for three nights, from the area adjacent to it; and this points to the specification of the place, not the specification of the duration. The apparent sense is that copper was made to flow for Solomon from its mine as a spring flowing like springs of water, as a sign of his prophethood. al-Khalil said: al-Qitr is molten copper. I say: its evidence is the reading of the one who read: "min qaṭrān" (from tar).

(And among the jinn were those who worked before him by the permission of their Lord) meaning by His command. (And whoever of them deviates from Our command) which We commanded him, of obedience to Solomon.

(We shall make him taste the punishment of the Blaze) meaning in the Hereafter, as said by most of the exegetes. It has also been said that this refers to this world; that Allah, exalted, appointed over them, as al-Suddi related, an angel holding a whip of fire, so whoever deviated from the command of Solomon, he would strike him with that whip, a blow from a place he could not see, and it would burn him. The word "min" (of) in "min al-jinn" is in the accusative position, in the sense of "and We subjected to him from the jinn those who work." It may also be in the nominative position, as was mentioned regarding "al-rīḥ."

**Issue one:** Concerning His words, Exalted is He: ﴿from sanctuaries (maharib) and statues (tamathil)﴾. The *mihrab* in the lexicon is every elevated place. It is also said of the place where one prays, "mihrab," because it ought to be raised and held in honour. Al-Dahhak said: "﴿from sanctuaries﴾, i.e., from mosques." Qatadah said the same. Mujahid said: "The *mahareeb* are below the palaces." Abu 'Ubaydah said: "The *mihrab* is the most noble of the houses of a dwelling." He said:

*"And what would it matter to him if you remembered, or [remembered] Unais,*
*Like gazelles of the sand in sanctuaries of kings."* [[The verse is by Imru' al-Qays. Al-aqyal means kings, singular qayl.]]

'Adiy ibn Zayd said:

*"Like ivory dolls in the sanctuaries, or like white [flowers]*
*In the meadow, whose blossom gleams."*

It is also said that the *mihrab* is that which is reached by stairs, like a fine upper chamber, as in His words: ﴿when they climbed over the wall into the sanctuary﴾ [[See vol. 15, p. 165.]] [Sad: 21], and His words: ﴿so he came out to his people from the sanctuary﴾ [[See vol. 11, p. 14.]] [Maryam: 11], meaning he came up to them. A report says that he [Sulayman] commanded that around his throne be made a thousand *mihrabs*, in each of which were a thousand men wearing woollen garments, crying out to God continually. He was on the throne in his procession, with the *mihrabs* around him. When he rode, he would say to his troops: "Glorify God up to that banner." When they reached it, he would say: "Declare His oneness up to that banner." When they reached it, he would say: "Magnify Him up to that other banner." So the troops would raise their glorification, declaration of oneness and magnification together in one rising voice.

**Issue two:** His words, ﴿and statues﴾: it is the plural of *timthal*, which is anything fashioned in the likeness of a form, whether of a living being or of a non-living thing. It is said that they were statues of glass, copper and marble, of things that are not living beings. It is mentioned that they were images of prophets and scholars, which were made in the mosques so that people would see them and increase in worship and diligence. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Those people, when a righteous man died among them, built a mosque over his grave and fashioned in it those images," [meaning] so that they would remember their worship and strive in worship. This indicates that image-making was permissible in that era, and this was abrogated (*naskh*, abrogation) by the law of Muhammad (ﷺ). More explanation of this will come in the surah of "Nuh" (peace be upon him). [[See vol. 18, p. 307 onwards.]] It is also said: the *tamathil* were talismans which he made, and he forbade every image-maker from going beyond them, so none would go beyond them. He would make a statue of a fly, or of a gnat, or of crocodiles, in a place, and would order them not to go beyond it, and no one ever went beyond it as long as that statue stood. The singular of *tamathil* is *timthal*, with a kasra on the ta'. He said:

*"And many a day I have enjoyed, and a night,*
*With a lovely maiden, as if she were the line of a statue."* [[The verse is by Imru' al-Qays.]]

It is also said: these statues were men whom he made of copper, and he asked his Lord to breathe the spirit into them so that they would fight in the way of God and the weapon would not wound them (*yahik*: it leaves its mark and effect). It is said that Isfandiyar was one of them, and God knows best. It is reported that they made for him two lions at the base of his throne and two eagles above it. When he wished to ascend, the two lions would spread their forelegs for him, and when he sat, the two eagles would unfurl their wings.

**Issue three:** Makki, in his *al-Hidayah*, relates that a group permits image-making and argues from this verse. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "That is an error, and I do not know of anyone among the imams of knowledge who permits it." I say: what Makki related was mentioned earlier by al-Nahhas. Al-Nahhas said: "A people said: the making of images is permissible because of this verse, and because of what God, Mighty and Majestic, related about the Messiah. Other people said: the prohibition from the Prophet (ﷺ) regarding them is authentic, and the threat against whoever makes them or takes them is authentic. So God, Mighty and Majestic, abrogated by this what had been permissible before it. The wisdom in that is that he (peace be upon him) was sent when images were being worshipped, so the more correct course was to remove them."

**Issue four:** The statue is of two kinds: living and non-living. The non-living is of two kinds: inanimate and sleeping [i.e., plant-like]. The jinn used to make for Sulayman all of these, because of the generality of His words: ﴿and statues﴾. In the Israelite narratives it is reported that statues of birds were on the throne of Sulayman. If it is said: there is no generality in His words ﴿and statues﴾, since it is an affirmation in an indefinite noun, and an affirmation in an indefinite noun has no generality; generality is only in a negation in an indefinite noun. We say: that is so, but this affirmation in an indefinite noun has been joined with what requires it to be taken as general, namely His words ﴿whatever he willed﴾, so the joining of *al-mashi'ah* (the will) to it requires its generality. If it is said: how did he permit the forbidden images? We say: that was permissible in his law, and it was abrogated by our law, as we have explained. And God knows best. Abu al-'Aliyah reported: making images was not forbidden at that time.

**Issue five:** What the hadiths imply is that images are prohibited. Then came (the exception) "except what is an embroidered design (*raqm*) on a garment," so it was singled out from the general body of images. Then dislike of it was established by his words (ﷺ) to 'A'ishah concerning the garment: "Remove it from me, for whenever I see it I remember this world." Then, by his tearing (*hatk*, ripping) the image-bearing garment from 'A'ishah he forbade it, and then by her cutting it into two cushions the image was altered and departed from its form. The permissibility of that is when the image on it is not in its complete form. If the image were in its complete form it would not be permissible, due to her saying regarding the image-bearing cushion (*numruqah*): "I bought it for you so that you may sit on it and recline on it," and he forbade it and threatened for it. It becomes clear from the hadith of praying toward images that it was permissible in an embroidered design on a garment, then the prohibition of it abrogated that. Thus the matter has settled, and God knows best. Ibn al-'Arabi said this.

**Issue six:** Muslim related from 'A'ishah: "We had a curtain with an image of a bird on it, and whoever entered would face it. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: 'Move this away, for whenever I enter and see it I remember this world.'" She said: "We had a woollen cloak whose edging we used to say was silk, and we used to wear it." And from her: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) came in while I was covered with a thin curtain (*qiram*) that had an image on it, and his face changed colour. Then he took hold of the curtain and tore it, then said: 'Among the people most severely punished on the Day of Resurrection are those who imitate the creation of God, Mighty and Majestic.'" And from her: she had a garment with images extended to a *sahwah* [[a small recess sloping slightly into the ground, resembling an alcove or closet. It is also said to be a porch in front of the house. It is also said to be like a shelf or niche in which a thing is placed.]], and the Prophet (ﷺ) used to pray facing it. He said: "Move it away from me." She said: "I moved it and made it into two cushions." Some scholars said: it is possible that his tearing of the garment and his command to move it was out of scrupulousness, because the station of prophethood and messengerhood is perfection. So reflect on this.

**Issue seven:** Al-Muzani reported from al-Shafi'i: If a man is invited to a wedding feast and sees a figure with a soul, or figures with souls, he does not enter if they are set up (displayed). If they are to be trodden upon, there is no harm, and likewise if they are images of trees. They did not disagree that images on hanging curtains are disliked but not forbidden. Likewise, according to them, what is carved or engraved in a building. Some of them excepted "what is an embroidered design on a garment," on account of the hadith of Sahl ibn Hunayf. I say: the Messenger of God (ﷺ) cursed the image-makers and did not make an exception. And his words: "The people of these images will be punished on the Day of Resurrection, and it will be said to them: 'Give life to what you have created'" — he made no exception. In al-Tirmidhi, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "A neck (*'unuq*: a piece) will come out of the Fire on the Day of Resurrection, having two eyes that see and two ears that hear and a tongue that speaks, saying: 'I have been charged with three: with every tyrannical obstinate person, with everyone who calls upon another god alongside God, and with the image-makers.'" Abu 'Isa said: this is a good, strange, sound hadith. In al-Bukhari and Muslim, from 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, who said: the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "The people most severely punished on the Day of Resurrection are the image-makers." This indicates the prohibition of making an image of anything whatsoever. And He, Mighty and Majestic, has said: ﴿You could not have made its trees grow﴾ [[See vol. 13, p. 219.]] [An-Naml: 60], according to what has already been explained, so know this.

**Issue eight:** It has been excepted from this category the toys of girls, because it is established that 'A'ishah, may God be pleased with her, was married to the Prophet (ﷺ) when she was seven years old, and she was brought to him when she was nine, and she played with her dolls with him, and he died leaving her when she was eighteen. Also from her, she said: "I used to play with dolls in the presence of the Prophet (ﷺ), and I had girlfriends who played with me. When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) entered, they would hide from him (*yanqami'na*: they would withdraw and enter a room or behind a curtain out of shyness and awe of him, peace be upon him), and he would send them (*yusarribuhunna*: send and dispatch them) to me, and they would play with me." Muslim recorded both reports. The scholars said: that was due to the necessity and the need of girls, so that they might train themselves in raising their children. Then, such things do not last, and likewise what is made of sweets or of dough does not last, so it was permitted. And God knows best.

**His words, Exalted is He: ﴿and bowls like cisterns (al-jawab)﴾.** Ibn 'Arafah said: *al-jawabi* is the plural of *al-jabiyah*, which is a pit like a basin. He also said: like the watering troughs of camels. Ibn al-Qasim reported from Malik: like a hollow in the ground. The meanings are close. A thousand men would sit around a single bowl. Al-Nahhas said: "*wa-jifanin ka-al-jawab*": it is preferable that it be with a *ya'*; whoever omits the *ya'* says that the proper way is for *alif-lam* to enter upon an indefinite noun without changing its state, and since it was said *jawab* and the *alif-lam* entered, it remained in its state, so the *ya'* was dropped. The singular of *al-jawabi* is *jabiyah*, which is a large cooking pot, and a large great basin in which something is collected (*yujba*), i.e., gathered. From this comes *jabaytu al-kharaj* (I collected the tax) and *jabaytu al-jarad* (I gathered the locusts), meaning I made a cloak and gathered them into it. However, Layth reported from Mujahid who said: *al-jawabi* is the plural of *jawbah*, and the *jawbah* is a large hollow that is in a mountain, in which is rainwater. Al-Kisa'i said: *jabawtu al-ma'* in the basin and *jabaytuhu*, i.e., I gathered it, and the *jabiyah* is the basin in which water is gathered for camels. He said:

*"It goes forth over the family of al-Muhallaq, a bowl*
*Like the cistern of the old Iraqi man, overflowing."* [[The verse is by al-A'sha. Al-fahaq means fullness. He specified the Iraqi because of his ignorance of waters, since he is a townsman: when he finds water, he fills his cistern and prepares for it, not knowing when he will find water again. As for the Bedouin, he knows the waters, so he is not concerned whether he prepares for them.]]

It is also narrated:

*"It denies blame from the family of al-Muhallaq, a bowl*
*Like the cistern of flowing water ....*"

Al-Nahhas mentioned this.

**His words, Exalted is He: ﴿and fixed cooking pots﴾.** Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: they are copper cooking pots that were in Persia. Al-Dahhak said: they are cooking pots made from mountains. Others said: they have been hewn from solid mountains, of what the devils made for him; their tripods are likewise hewn from mountains. The meaning of *rasiyat* is fixed, not moved and not shifted, because of their enormity. Ibn al-'Arabi said: likewise were the cooking pots of 'Abdullah ibn Jud'an, to which one would ascend by a ladder in the pre-Islamic period. Tarafah ibn al-'Abd alluded to them with his words:

*"Like the cisterns, never ceasing to be filled*
*For the hospitality of guests, or for the one in need."*

Ibn al-Arabi said: I also saw in the ribat of Abu Sa'id the cooking pots of the Sufis in a similar manner: they all cook together and all eat together, with none of them monopolising anything for himself over anyone else.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Work, O family of Dawud, in gratitude; and few of My servants are grateful.﴾ The meaning of gratitude (shukr) has already passed in al-Baqarah [[See vol. 1, p. 397 onward.]] and elsewhere. It is related that the Prophet ﷺ climbed the pulpit, recited this verse, and then said: (Whoever is given three things has been given the like of what was given to the family of Dawud.) He said: We said: "What are they?" He said: (Justice in contentment and anger; moderation in poverty and wealth; and fear of Allah in secret and in public.) At-Tirmidhi al-Hakim, Abu 'Abd Allah, narrated it from Ata' ibn Yasar from Abu Hurayrah.

It is also related that Dawud, peace be upon him, said: (My Lord, how can I bear to thank You for Your blessings? My being inspired and my power to thank You are themselves a blessing from You.) He said: (O Dawud, now you have known Me.) This meaning has passed in Surah Ibrahim [[See vol. 9, p. 343.]].

The reality of gratitude is acknowledging the blessing as coming from the Benefactor and employing it in His obedience, while ingratitude (kufran) is employing it in disobedience. Few do this, because good is less than evil and obedience is less than disobedience, according to the prior decree.

Mujahid said: When Allah, exalted is He, said, "Work, O family of Dawud, in gratitude," Dawud said to Sulayman: "Indeed Allah, mighty and majestic, has mentioned gratitude, so relieve me of the prayer of the day and I will relieve you of the prayer of the night." He said: "I cannot." He said: "Then relieve me—" al-Faryabi said: "I think he said, until the midday prayer." He said: "Yes," and so he relieved him.

Al-Zuhri said: "Work, O family of Dawud, in gratitude" means: say, "All praise is for Allah." And "gratitude" (shukran) is in the accusative as an object, meaning: do a deed which is gratitude. It is as if prayer, fasting and all acts of worship are in themselves gratitude, since they fill its place. This is clarified by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Except those who believe and do righteous deeds, and they are few﴾ [[See vol. 15, p. 165 onward.]] [p. 24], and this is what is meant by His saying, "and few of My servants are grateful." Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah, in interpreting His saying, ﴿Be grateful to Me﴾ [Luqman: 14], said that gratitude here means the five daily prayers.

In Sahih Muslim, it is narrated from 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ would stand in prayer at night until his feet cracked [[Tafattara: to split open.]]. 'A'ishah said to him: "Do you do this when Allah has forgiven you what came before of your sins and what came after?" He said: (Shall I not be a grateful servant?). Muslim alone narrated it.

The apparent meaning of the Qur'an and the Sunnah is that gratitude is by the deeds of the body, not limited to the deed of the tongue; so gratitude by actions is the deed of the limbs, and gratitude by words is the deed of the tongue. And Allah knows best.

His saying: ﴿And few of My servants are grateful﴾ may be addressed to the family of Dawud, and may be addressed to Muhammad ﷺ. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: In every case there is in it a warning and an exhortation. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, heard a man say: "O Allah, make me of the few," and 'Umar said: "What is this supplication?" The man said: "I meant His saying, 'and few of My servants are grateful.'" 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Everyone knows better than you, O 'Umar!"

It is related that Sulayman, peace be upon him, used to eat barley and feed his family khushkar [[Khushkar: coarse flour (Persian).]] and feed the poor darmak [[Darmak: fine flour, the white flour.]]. It has also been said that he used to eat ashes and use them as a pillow, but the first is more sound, since ashes are not food. It is related that he never ate his fill, and when he was asked about that he said: "I fear that if I eat my fill I will forget the hungry." This is from gratitude and from the few. So reflect on it, and Allah knows best.

**The commentary of al-Qurtubi on the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Then when We decreed death for him﴾**

Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿So when We decreed death for him﴾, meaning: when We ruled over Sulayman with death, until it became a settled matter and death befell him. ﴿Nothing showed them his death except a creature of the earth eating away at his staff﴾. This was because he was leaning on his staff (*al-minsa'ah*, which in the language of Abyssinia means the staff, according to al-Suddi; it is said to be in the language of Yemen, as mentioned by al-Qushayri). So he died in that position, and his condition remained hidden until he fell down dead, because the staff had been broken by the earth-creature eating it. His death was then known through this. Thus the earth-creature was a sign of his death, meaning a cause for his death to become apparent. He had asked Allah, the Exalted, that they not learn of his death until a year had passed over him.

The scholars differed about the reason for his request, on two views. The first is what Qatadah and others said: The jinn used to claim knowledge of the unseen. When Sulayman, peace be upon him, died and his death was hidden from them, "the jinn realised that had they known the unseen, they would not have remained in the humiliating punishment." Ibn Mas'ud said: He remained for a year while the jinn were working before him, until the earth-creature ate his staff and he fell. It is also reported that when he fell, they did not know since his death. The earth-creature was placed on the staff, and it ate from it for a day and a night. Then they calculated and found that he had died a year earlier.

It was also said: The chiefs of the jinn were seven, and they were subject to Sulayman, peace be upon him. Dawud, peace be upon him, had founded the Bayt al-Maqdis (the Holy House in Jerusalem). When he died, he bequeathed to Sulayman the completion of the mosque of Bayt al-Maqdis, so Sulayman commanded the jinn to it. When his death drew near, he said to his family: "Do not inform them of my death until they complete the building of the mosque," and a year remained for its completion.

In a report, the Angel of Death was his friend, and he asked him about the sign of his death. He said: "A tree called the *kharnubah* will grow from the place of your prostration." So there was not a day he woke up in which a tree did not sprout in Bayt al-Maqdis. He would ask it: "What is your name?" The tree would say: "My name is such and such." He would say: "For what purpose are you?" It would say: "For such and such." He would then order it to be cut down, plant it in an orchard of his, and order that its benefits, harms, name, and medicinal uses be written down. Then one day, while he was praying, he saw a tree that had grown before him. He said to it: "What is your name?" It said: "The *kharnubah*." He said: "For what purpose are you?" It said: "For the ruin of this mosque." Sulayman said: "Allah would not ruin it while I am alive! It is you who are destined for my destruction and the destruction of Bayt al-Maqdis!" So he uprooted it and planted it in his garden, then said: "O Allah, conceal my death from the jinn, so that mankind may know that the jinn do not know the unseen." The jinn used to report that they knew some of the unseen and knew what was to come. Then he put on his shroud, applied perfume, entered the prayer niche (*mihrab*), stood to pray, and leaned on his staff upon his seat. He died, and the jinn did not know until a year had passed and the building of the mosque was completed.

Abu Ja'far al-Nahhas said: "This is the best of what has been said concerning the verse." Its soundness is supported by the attributed (*marfu'*) hadith which Ibrahim ibn Tahman narrated from Ata' ibn al-Sa'ib, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn Abbas, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "The prophet of Allah, Sulayman son of Dawud, peace be upon them both, when he prayed, would see a tree growing before him, and he would ask it, 'What is your name?' If it was for planting, it would be planted; if it was for medicine, it would be recorded. Then one day, while he was praying, a tree grew before him, and he said, 'What is your name?' It said, 'The *kharnubah*.' He said, 'For what purpose are you?' It said, 'For the ruin of this house.' He said, 'O Allah, conceal my death from the jinn, until mankind knows that the jinn do not know the unseen.' So they carved it into a staff, and he leaned on it for a year without them knowing. Then it fell, and mankind knew that the jinn do not know the unseen, so they looked at the time that had passed and found it to be a year."

In the recitation of Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn Abbas: "The humankind realised that had the jinn known the unseen..." Ya'qub, in the transmission of Ruways, recited "tabayyanat al-jinnu" (the jinn realised) with the subject unnamed. Nafi' and Abu Amr recited "ta'kulu minsatahu" with an *alif* between the *sin* and the *ta'*, without a *hamzah*. The rest recited it with an open *hamzah* in place of the *alif*. Both are valid dialectal forms. However, Ibn Dhakwan softened the *hamzah* by making it silent for lightness. A poet used the form without *hamzah*:

"When you walk upon the staff from old age,
then pleasure and romance have moved far from you."

Another poet used the form with an open *hamzah*:

"We struck his face with a staff,
so he became humiliated and abased by it."

Another said:

"Was it for the sake of a rope—may your father not be safe—that you struck him
with a staff, when your rope has dragged out its strands?"

Another poet softened its *hamzah*:

"One standing, who has risen from his reclining,
like an old man's rising to his staff."

Its root is from *nasa'tu al-ghanam*, meaning I drove the sheep and herded them, so the staff was named thus because something is driven and herded with it. Tarafah said:

"Trustworthy like the planks of a bier, I drove them
along a clear path, as if it were the back of a striped cloak."

[Note: *al-amun* is the camel one trusts not to stumble. *Al-iran* is the coffin of the dead. *Al-lahib* is the clear road. *Al-burjud* is a striped garment.]

Here he softened its *hamzah*. Al-Nahhas said: Its derivation shows that it is spelled with *hamzah*, since it derives from *nasa'tuhu*, meaning I delayed him and pushed him away. It is called *minsa'ah* because something is pushed away and delayed with it. Mujahid and Ikrimah said: It is the staff. Then the one who recited *minsatahu* replaced the *hamzah* with an *alif*.

If it is asked: substitution of *hamzah* is very ugly and only permissible in poetry, far-fetched and irregular, and Abu Amr ibn al-Ala' would not overlook such a thing, especially as the people of Medina use this recitation. The answer to this is that the Arabs used substitution in this word and pronounced it thus, as substitution occurs in other words, though it is not analogical. Abu Ubayd said: "I do not know by whom it was narrated, except that it is not spelled with *hamzah*, because what was spelled with *hamzah* may have its *hamzah* dropped, but what was not spelled with *hamzah* may not have *hamzah* added in any way." Al-Mahdawi said: Whoever recites with a silent *hamzah* is irregular and far-fetched, because before the feminine *ha'* only a vowelled letter or an *alif* can precede it. However, it is permissible that what was vowelled with an open vowel was made silent for lightness, and it is permissible that when they substituted the *hamzah* with an *alif* without analogy, they turned the *alif* back into a *hamzah*, as they did in their saying *al-'alim* and *al-khatim*.

It is narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr that he read *min* separated, and *sa'atihi* with a *hamzah* and a vowel of *kasrah* on the *ta'*. It was said: It is from *si'at al-qaws* (the bowstring's curve) in the dialect of one who pronounces the *hamzah*. It is reported that Ru'bah pronounced *sima'at al-qaws* with a *hamzah*. Al-Jawhari said: *Siyat al-qaws* is what is bent from its two ends, its plural is *siyat*, and the *ha'* is a substitute for the *waw*, and the relative form of it is *siyawi*. Abu Ubaydah said: Ru'bah used to pronounce *siyat al-qaws* with a *hamzah*, while the rest of the Arabs did not pronounce it so.

Concerning "the creature of the earth," there are two views. The first: it is the *arḍah* (woodworm), said by Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, and others. It has been recited as "*dabbat al-arad*" with an open *ra'*, which is the plural of *al-arḍah*, mentioned by al-Mawardi. The second: it is a creature that eats wood. Al-Jawhari said: *Al-arḍah* (with a vowel on the *ra'*) is a small creature that eats wood. It is said: "The wood was *uriḍat*, *tu'raḍu arḍan*" (with a silent *ra'*), so it is *ma'rūḍah* when it has been eaten.

Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿So when he fell﴾, meaning, collapsed. ﴿The jinn realised﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: That is, the jinn realised his death. Others said: The meaning is that the matter of the jinn became clear, like ﴿and ask the town﴾ [Yusuf: 82]. In the exegesis, with sound chains from Ibn Abbas, he said: Sulayman son of Dawud, peace and blessings be upon them both, remained for a year with his death unknown, while he was leaning on his staff, and the jinn were going about in the tasks he had commanded them. Then he fell after a year. ﴿So when he fell, the humankind realised that had the jinn known the unseen, they would not have remained in the humiliating punishment.﴾ This recitation from Ibn Abbas is by way of exegesis.

In a report: the jinn thanked the earth-creature for this, so wherever it was, they would bring it water. Al-Suddi said: "And clay, do you not see the clay that is inside wood? The devils bring it to it in gratitude." It said: "If you were eating food and drink, we would have brought them to you."

The word *anna* (that) is in the nominative position as a substitute for *al-jinn*, and the estimate is: the matter of the jinn became clear, so the noun was omitted, meaning it became clear and manifest to humankind and was revealed to them that the matter of the jinn is that they do not know the unseen. This is a substitution of inclusion (*badal al-ishtimal*). It may also be in the accusative position with the omission of the preposition.

*Labithu* means they remained. *Al-adhab al-muhin* (the humiliating punishment) means forced labour, carrying, building, and other such things.

Sulayman lived fifty-three years, and his reign lasted forty years. He became king at thirteen and began building Bayt al-Maqdis at seventeen. Al-Suddi and others said: Sulayman's age was sixty-seven [sic: the text reads "sixty-seven" as "seven and sixty"]. He became king at seventeen and began building Bayt al-Maqdis at twenty, and his reign was fifty years.

It is related that Sulayman, peace be upon him, began building Bayt al-Maqdis in the fourth year of his reign, and after finishing it he offered twelve thousand bulls and one hundred and twenty thousand sheep, and made the day he finished its building a festival. He stood upon the rock, raising his hands to Allah, the Exalted, in supplication, and said: "O Allah, You granted me this dominion and strengthened me to build this mosque. O Allah, inspire me to thank You for what You have bestowed upon me, let me die upon Your religion, and do not let my heart swerve after You have guided me. O Allah, I ask You for those who enter this mosque five qualities: no sinner who enters it seeking repentance will leave without You forgiving him and accepting his repentance; no one fearful, but You will grant him security; no one sick, but You will heal him; no one poor, but You will enrich him. And the fifth: that You do not turn Your gaze away from whoever enters it until he leaves, except those who intend deviation or wrongdoing. O Lord of the worlds!" Al-Mawardi mentioned this.

I say: This is more sound than what preceded it, that the building was not completed until a year after his death. The evidence for its soundness is what al-Nasa'i and others transmitted with a sound chain from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Amr, from the Prophet (ﷺ): "When Sulayman son of Dawud built Bayt al-Maqdis, he asked Allah, the Exalted, for three things: a judgment that would coincide with His judgment, so he was granted it; a dominion that would not be fitting for anyone after him, so he was granted it; and when he finished building the mosque, he asked Allah that no one would come to it who has nothing driving him to it except prayer in it, but that he would leave his sin like the day his mother bore him." We have mentioned this hadith in *Al 'Imran* [see vol. 4, p. 137], and we mentioned its building in *Subhan* [see vol. 10, p. 211].

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 34, verse 15:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿There was certainly for Sheba, in their dwelling-place, a sign﴾ [[(في مساكنهم) This is the reading of Nafi', and it is the reading with which the author (may God have mercy on him) used to recite.]]

Nafi' and others read it with diptote inflection (al-sarf) and tanwin, treating it as the name of a man (ism hayy), and it was originally a man's name. This was transmitted from the Prophet (ﷺ). Al-Tirmidhi related: Abu Kurayb and Abd ibn Humayd told us, both saying: Abu Usamah told us, from al-Hasan ibn al-Hakam al-Nakha'i, who said: Abu Sabrah al-Nakha'i told us, from Farwah ibn Musayk al-Muradi, who said: I came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "O Messenger of God, shall I not fight those of my people who have turned their backs with those of them who have turned toward (Islam)?" So he gave me permission to fight them and appointed me commander. When I left his presence, he asked about me: "What has al-Ghutayfi done?" [[In the originals and in al-Tirmidhi: "al-Qutayfi" with a qaf instead of a ghayn, which is a distortion.]] He was informed that I had set out. He said: "So he sent after me and brought me back, and I came to him while he was among a group of his companions, and he said: 'Call the people. Whoever among them has embraced Islam, accept from him, and whoever has not embraced Islam, do not hasten until I renew my instruction to you.'" He said: "And there was revealed concerning Saba' what was revealed." A man said: "O Messenger of God, what is Saba'? Is it a land or a woman?" He said: "It is neither a land nor a woman, but it is a man who fathered ten of the Arabs; six of them went to the right (tayammana) and four of them went to the left (tashalanguage)..." Those who went to the left were Lakhm, Judham, Ghassan and Amilah. Those who went to the right were al-Azd, al-Ash'ariyyun, Himyar, Kindah, Madhhij and Anmar. A man said: "O Messenger of God, and what is Anmar?" He said: "Those from whom are Khath'am and Bajilah." This is also related from Ibn Abbas, from the Prophet (ﷺ). Abu Isa said: This is a hasan gharib hadith.

Ibn Kathir and Abu Amr read "li-Saba'" without diptote inflection, making it the name of a tribe. This is the choice of Abu Ubayd, and he argued that it is the name of a tribe because what follows is "in their dwellings" (fi masakinihim). Al-Nahhas said: Had it been as he said, it would have been "in their dwellings" (fi masakinaha, feminine). The meaning has been further explained in "al-Naml" [[See vol. 13, p. 181]].

The poet said, using the diptote form:

"Those who came down, and Taym, on the heights of Saba', the buffalo hide has bitten their necks."

Another said, in the form without inflection:

"From Saba', those who were present in Ma'rib, when they were building, beyond its flood, the dam (al-'aram)."

Qunbul, Abu Hanifah and al-Jahdari read "li-Saba'" with the hamzah sukun. "In their dwelling-place" (fi masakinihim) is the reading of the common readers, in the plural, and it is the choice of Abu Ubayd and Abu Hatim, because they had many dwellings and it was not a single dwelling. Ibrahim, Hamzah and Hafs read "maskanihim" in the singular, except that they vowelled the kaf with a fatha. Yahya, al-A'mash and al-Kisa'i read it in the singular likewise, except that they vowelled the kaf with a kasra. Al-Nahhas said: The one with sukun (the unvowelled form) is clearer in this, because it unites the wording and the meaning. When you say "maskanihim," there are two possibilities: one, that it is a singular that serves for the plural; the other, that it is a verbal noun (masdar) which is neither dualised nor pluralised, as God the Exalted says: ﴿God has sealed their hearts and their hearing and over their eyes﴾ [[See vol. 1, p. 185]] [al-Baqarah: 7], where He used "hearing" in the singular. Likewise ﴿a seat of truthfulness﴾ [[See vol. 17, p. 149]] [al-Qamar: 55]. "Maskin" is like "masjid," an anomaly outside analogy, and its like is found only by transmission.

"A sign" (ayah) is the subject of kana, meaning a clear indication pointing to God the Exalted's power, that they have a Creator who created them, and that if all creatures gathered together to bring forth a fruit from a piece of wood, they would not be able to do so; and they would not have been guided to the variety of the kinds of fruits, their colours, flavours, scents and blossoms. In that is what shows that these cannot come except from a knowing, powerful Lord.

(Two gardens) may be a substitute (badal) for "a sign," and it may be the predicate of a deleted subject, in which case stopping at "a sign" on this reading is not a complete pause. Al-Zajjaj said: That is, the sign is two gardens; "two gardens" is in the nominative because it is the predicate of a deleted subject. Al-Farra' said: It is in the nominative as an explanation of "a sign," and "a sign" may be in the accusative as the predicate of kana, and "the two gardens" may be in the accusative as predicate as well, outside the Qur'an.

Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd said: The sign that was for the people of Saba' in their dwellings was that they never saw in it a gnat, nor a fly, nor a flea, nor a louse, nor a scorpion, nor a snake, nor any other of the vermin; and when a caravan came to them with lice and insects in their clothes, when they looked at their houses the insects died. It was also said: The sign was the two gardens; a woman would walk between them with a basket (mikhtal) on her head, and it would fill with all kinds of fruits without her touching them with her hand. This was said by Qatadah. It is related that the two gardens were between two mountains in Yemen. Sufyan said: Two palaces were found in them, one of which had written on it: "We built Salhin in seventy autumns, working continually," and on the other was written: "We built Sirwah, a resting place and a pasture." One of the two gardens was on the right of the valley and the other on its left. Al-Qushayri said: He did not mean two gardens only, but rather from the two gardens on the right and the left; that is, their lands were full of orchards, trees and fruits, and people sheltered in their shade.

"Eat of the provision of your Lord" means: it was said to them, "Eat," and there was no command there, but they had access to those blessings. It was also said: The messengers said to them that God the Exalted had permitted them this, that is, He has permitted you these blessings, so give thanks to Him by obedience.

(Of the provision of your Lord): that is, of the fruits of the two gardens.

(And give thanks to Him): meaning for what He has provided you.

(A good land): this is a resumed statement, meaning: this is a good land, that is, abundant in fruits. It was also said: not salt-marshy. It was also said: good, having no vermin because of the goodness of its air. Mujahid said: It is Sana'a.

(And a Lord Forgiving): that is, the One who bestows these upon you is a Lord Forgiving who covers your sins. Thus He combined for them forgiveness of their sins and the goodness of their land, and He did not combine this for all of His creation. It was also said: He mentioned forgiveness only to indicate that provision may contain what is unlawful. The discussion of this has passed at the beginning of "al-Baqarah" [[See vol. 1, p. 177]]. It was also said: He bestowed favour upon them by pardoning them from the punishment of extirpation, for having denied the earlier prophets whom they had denied, until they persisted in obstinacy and were uprooted.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 34, verse 16:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So they turned away﴾, meaning: from His command and from following His messengers, after they had been submitting (muslimin).

Al-Suddi and Wahb said: He sent to the people of Saba' thirteen prophets, and they denied them.

Al-Qushayri said: They had a chief who was nicknamed "the Donkey," and they lived in the time of the fatrah (the interval without messengers) between Jesus and Muhammad, may Allah bless them both and grant them peace.

It was said: He had a son who died, so he raised his head to the sky, spat, and disbelieved. For this reason it is said: "More disbelieving than a donkey."

Al-Jawhari said: Their saying "More disbelieving than a donkey" refers to a man from 'Ad whose sons died, so he disbelieved with a great disbelief. No one passed through his land without his calling them to disbelief; if they answered, well, and if not, he killed them. Then, when the flood ran through their two gardens, they scattered throughout the lands, as its explanation will come. For this reason it is said in the proverb: "They scattered like the hands of Saba'" (tafarraqu ayadi Saba'). It was also said: the Aws and the Khazraj are from them.

(﴿So We sent upon them the flood of al-'Arim﴾) As for al-'Arim, it was reported from Ibn 'Abbas that it is the dam, so the reading is: the flood of the great dam (al-sadd al-'Arim). 'Ata' said: al-'Arim is the name of the valley. Qatadah said: al-'Arim is the valley of Saba', into which the torrents of the valleys gathered, it was said from the sea and the valleys of Yemen. They built a barrier between two mountains and made in that barrier three gates, one above another. They would irrigate from the highest, then from the second, then from the third, according to their needs. Thus they became fertile and their wealth multiplied. When they denied the messengers, Allah sent the mouse upon them, and it gnawed through the barrier.

Wahb said: They used to claim that in their knowledge and their soothsaying they found that a mouse would destroy their dam. So they left no gap between two rocks without tying a cat to its side. When what Allah the Exalted intended for them came, a red mouse approached one of those cats and attacked it until it drew back from the rock. Then it leapt and entered the gap that was beside it, and gnawed through the dam until it weakened it for the flood, while they did not know. When the flood came, it entered those cracks until it reached the dam, and the water overflowed onto their property, drowning it and burying their houses.

Al-Zajjaj said: al-'Arim is the name of the rat that gnawed through the dyke (sikr) upon them, and it is what is called al-khuld. Qatadah also said this. So the flood was attributed to it because it was the cause. Ibn al-A'rabi also said: al-'Arim is among the names of the mouse.

Mujahid and Ibn Abi Najih said: al-'Arim is a red water that Allah the Exalted sent into the dam, so it split and demolished it. And it is reported from Ibn 'Abbas also that al-'Arim is the violent rain. It was also said: al-'Arm, with the ra' sukun.

From al-Dahhak: they were in the fatrah between Jesus and Muhammad, peace be upon them both.

'Amr ibn Shurahbil said: al-'Arim is the musannah (dam/embankment), and al-Jawhari said the same, and he said: it has no singular from its own form, and it is said its singular is 'arimah. Muhammad ibn Yazid said: al-'Arim is every thing that serves as a barrier between two things, and it is what is called al-sikr, and it is the plural of 'arimah. Al-Nahhas said: what gathers of rain between two mountains, with a musannah at its face, is al-'Arim, and the musannah is what the people of Egypt call al-jisr (the bridge/dam), and they would open it whenever they wished, and when their two gardens were watered, they would close it. Al-Harawi said: al-musannah is the dam built against a flood to turn it back; it was called musannah because in it are the keys of the water. It is related that al-'Arim was a dam built by Bilqis, the queen of Sulayman, peace be upon him, and it is the musannah in the language of Himyar. She built it with rock and pitch, and made for it three gates, some above others. It is derived from al-'aramah, which is violence, and from it: a man 'arim, meaning fierce. And 'aramtu al-'azm (I stripped the bone) — u'rimuhu wa u'ruhu 'aran (I gnawed it clean) when I stripped it. Likewise, the camels 'aramat al-shajar, meaning they reached it. Al-'uram with a damma: the shreds of meat on the bone and the tree. And ta'arramtu al-'azm: I stripped the bone. A boy who is 'arim bayyin al-'uram (with a damma), meaning fierce. And he became 'arim, ya'rum and ya'rim, 'aramah (with a fatha). And al-'arim is al-'arim (the violent one), from al-Jawhari.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We replaced their two gardens with two gardens of bitter produce (khamt)﴾. Abu 'Amr read (ukuli khamtin) without tanwin, as an idafah. The people of tafsir and al-Khalil said: al-khamt is the arak (tree). Al-Jawhari: al-khamt is a kind of arak that has a fruit which is eaten. Abu 'Ubaydah said: it is every thriny tree that has bitterness in it. Al-Zajjaj: every plant that has bitterness such that it cannot be eaten. Al-Mubarrad: al-khamt is everything that has changed into what is not desired. Milk is khamt when it turns sour. The preferable reading in his view is "dhawatay ukulin khamtin" with tanwin, as an attribute of "ukulin" or as a substitute for it, because the ukul is, in his view, the khamt itself. As for the idafah, its permissibility may be that its estimate is "dhawatay ukuli humudatin" (two of sourness) or "ukuli marratin" (of bitterness). Al-Akhfash said: the idafah is more elegant in the speech of the Arabs, like their saying: thawb khazz (a garment of silk). Al-Khamt: sour milk. Abu 'Ubayd mentioned that when milk loses the sweetness of milking and its taste has not changed, it is samit; if it takes some of the scent, it is khamit and khamiit; if it takes some of the taste, it is mumahhal; when there is in it the taste of sweetness, it is fawwahah. Ibn Sidah's al-Mukhassas: (fawwahah, Sahib al-'Ayn: fawhah with fa'). In lexicons: al-qawhah (with damma): milk that has changed slightly and has sweetness in it. And al-fawhah (like qabrah): milk that has the taste of sweetness. Takhammata al-fahl: he roared. Takhammata fulan: he became angry and proud. Takhammata al-bahr: it crashed (the sea surged). Khamatu al-shah akhmituha khamtan: when I removed its skin and roasted it, it is khamit; if I removed its hair and roasted it, it is samit. And al-khamtah: wine that has taken on the scent of ripeness like the scent of apples and has not yet fully ripened. It is said it is the sour one, as said al-Jawhari. Al-Qutabi in Adab al-Katib said: the sour one is called khamtah. It is also said: khamtah is the one that has taken some of the scent. And he recited:

"A wine like the water of the Ni (a red wine), it is not khamtah, nor khallah, whose shihab (flame) burns the drinkers."

[Al-khallah: that which has exceeded its measure and passed from the state of wine to the state of sourness and vinegar. Al-shurub: the boon companions. He says: it is in the colour of the Ni meat.]

(And athl) Al-Farra' said: it is similar to the tamarisk (tarfa') except that it is taller than it, and from it is made the minbar of the Prophet ﷺ. The athl has thick roots from which doors are made, and its leaves are like those of the tamarisk. Its singular is athlah and its plural athlath. Al-Hasan said: al-athl is wood. Qatadah: it is a kind of wood resembling the tamarisk, which I saw in Fayd. It was said it is the samur (acacia). Abu 'Ubaydah said: it is the tree of al-nudar. [Al-nudar: gold, and al-nudar: wood from which bowls are made, and from it: a nudar cup.]

(And some lote-trees, few) Al-Farra' said: it is the samur, mentioned by al-Nahhas. Al-Azhari said: lote-trees (sidr) among trees are of two kinds: a wild one from which no benefit is gained, its leaves are not suitable for washing, and it has an astringent fruit that is not eaten, and this is what is called al-dal. The second is a sidr that grows on water, its fruit is the nabq (jujube), and its leaves are a washing agent, resembling the 'unnab tree. Qatadah said: whereas the trees of that people were among the best of trees, Allah the Exalted turned them into among the worst of trees because of their deeds; He destroyed their fruit-bearing trees and grew in their place the arak, the tamarisk, and the lote-tree. Al-Qushayri: the trees of the wilderness are not called a garden (jannah) or an orchard (bustan), but when the second was set against the first, the word jannah was applied, as in His saying: ﴿And the recompense for an evil deed is an evil deed like it﴾ [al-Shura: 40].
