It is possible that His saying "qalil" (few) refers to the whole of what was mentioned: the khamt, the athl, and the sidr.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 34, verse 17:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿That We recompensed them for their disbelief﴾, i.e., this alteration is the recompense for their disbelief. The position of "that" (dhalika) is accusative, meaning: We recompensed them that for their disbelief.

﴿And do We recompense any but the ungrateful?﴾ The recitation of the general body of readers is "yujaza" with a damma on the yaa and a fatha on the zay, and "al-kafur" in the nominative, as the verb is in the passive voice (lam yusamma fa'iluhu, the agent not named). Ya'qub, Hafs, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i recited "nujazi" with a nun and a kasra on the zay, and "al-kafura" in the accusative. This reading was preferred by Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim, who said: because before it is "jazaynahum" and he did not say "juzu" (they were recompensed). Al-Nahhas said: the matter in this is broad, and the meaning in it is clear; if one speaker said "God, exalted is He, created Adam ﷺ from clay," and another said "Adam was created from clay," the meaning would be one and the same.

Issue: In this verse there is a question which is no more severe in this surah than it, namely: why did God, exalted is He, restrict the recompense to the ungrateful and not mention the people of sins? The scholars spoke on this. Some said: no one is recompensed with this recompense, which is extirpation (al-istilam, i.e., uprooting) [[al-istilam: al-isti'sal, uprooting]] and destruction, except one who disbelieves. Mujahid said: "yujaza" means "yu'aqab" (is punished), because the believer has God expiate his misdeeds, while the disbeliever is recompensed for all the evil of his deeds; so the believer is "yujza" (rewarded) and is not "yujaza" because he is given reward (in the copy of the original: "la yuthab", "is not rewarded"). Tawus said: it is the scrutiny in the reckoning, and as for the believer, his reckoning is not scrutinized. Qutrub said something other than this: he took it to refer to the people of sins other than the disbelievers, and said: the meaning applies to one who denies the blessings and commits the major sins.

Al-Nahhas: The best of what has been said regarding this verse and the most magnificent of what has been related concerning it is that al-Hasan said: "Like for like." And on the authority of 'Aishah, may Allah be pleased with her, she said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "Whoever is brought to account is destroyed." I said: "O Prophet of Allah, then where is the saying of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿So he will be reckoned with an easy reckoning﴾ [al-Inshiqaq: 8]?" He said: "That is only the presentation (al-'ard), and whoever is scrutinized in the reckoning is destroyed." This is a sound chain of narration. Its explanation: the disbeliever is requited for his deeds and is called to account for them, and whatever good he did is nullified. This is confirmed by His saying, may He be exalted, in the first: "That We recompensed them for their disbelief," and in the second: "And do We recompense any but the ungrateful?" The meaning of "yujaza" is: he is requited for every deed he did, and the meaning of "jazaynahum" is: We requited them. This is the literal sense of the language, although "jaza" may occur in the sense of "jaza" (recompense) figuratively.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 34, verse 18:

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿And We placed between them and the towns which We had blessed, towns that were visible﴾. Al-Hasan said: meaning between Yemen and Syria. "The towns which We had blessed" are Syria, the Jordan and Palestine. As for the blessing: it is said that there were four thousand and seven hundred towns blessed with trees, fruit and water. It is also possible that "which We had blessed" refers to the abundance of their number.

(﴿towns that were visible﴾) Ibn Abbas said: he means between Medina and Syria. Qatadah said: the meaning of "visible" is: connected along a road, so that they would set out in the morning and take their midday rest in one town, and set out in the afternoon and spend the night in another town. It was also said: there was a town with a market at every mile, and this was the reason for the safety of the road. Al-Hasan said: a woman would go out with her spindle, and on her head her basket; she would busy herself with her spindle and would not return to her house until her basket was filled with all kinds of fruit, and so it was with the whole stretch between Syria and Yemen. It was also said that "visible" means "elevated," as said by al-Mubarrad. And it was said: they were called "visible" because of their visibility, that is, when you leave one, the next one becomes visible to you, so they were visible towns, that is, well known. It is said: "this is a visible matter," meaning well known.

(﴿And We appointed therein the stages of travel﴾) That is, We made the travel between their towns and the towns which We had blessed a measured journey from one station to another and from one town to another; that is, We made between every two towns a half day, so that the midday rest would be in one town and the night's lodging in another town. A person only exerts himself in travel due to lack of provisions and water and fear of the road; when he finds provisions and security, he does not burden himself with hardship, and he halts wherever he wishes.

(﴿Travel therein﴾) That is, and We said to them: travel therein, that is, in this distance. This is a command of permission, meaning they would travel in it to their destinations, when they wished, in security. It is a command with the sense of a statement, and it contains an implied verb of saying.

(﴿nights and days﴾) Two adverbial expressions. "In security" is in the accusative as a circumstantial state. He said "nights and days" in indefinite form to indicate the shortness of their journeys, that is, they had no need of long travel because of the availability of what they needed. Qatadah said: they would travel without fear, neither hungry nor thirsty, and they would travel a distance of four months in security, with none stirring another; even if a man met the murderer of his father, he would not touch him.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 34, verse 19:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So they said, "Our Lord, make the distances between our journeys farther apart"﴾. When they became insolent and overbearing, grew weary of ease, and were not patient with well-being, they wished for long journeys and toil in earning a living. This is like the saying of the Children of Israel: ﴿Then call upon your Lord for us to bring forth for us of what the earth grows: its herbs...﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:61], and the rest of the verse.[[See vol. 1, p. 422 onward.]] It is also like al-Nadr ibn al-Harith when he said: ﴿O Allah, if this is indeed the truth from You, then rain down upon us stones from the sky﴾ [al-Anfal 8:32].[[See vol. 8, p. (398).]] Allah answered him, and he was killed by the sword in cold blood on the day of Badr. (Qatl sabran, "killing in cold blood," is said of a man whose hands and feet are bound, or whom another man holds, until his neck is struck, or who is confined for execution until he is killed.) Likewise, these people were scattered throughout the world and torn into every tattered shred. Between them and al-Sham (Greater Syria) were placed deserts and wastelands, in which they ride mounts and take provisions for the journey.

The common reading is "Rabbana" with a fatha (naṣb), as a vocative construction (nida' mudaf, "addressed with a possessive suffix"), and it is in the accusative because it is the object (maf'ul bihi), since its meaning is: "I called and I invoked." "Ba'id" means that they asked for their journeys to be made more distant. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Ibn Muhaysin and Hisham, on the authority of Ibn 'Amir, read "Rabbana" in the same way, as a supplication, and "ba''id" with tashdid on the 'ayn, from al-ta'bid (causing distance). Al-Nahhas said: "Ba'id and ba''id have the same meaning, just as you say qarib and qarrib (both meaning 'bring near')."

Abu Salih, Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyya, Abu al-'Aliya, Nasr ibn 'Asim and Ya'qub read "Rabbuna" in the nominative (raf'), and "ba'ada" with a fatha on the 'ayn and the dal, as a statement (khabar). Its implied sense: "Our Lord has indeed made the distances between our journeys far apart." It is as if Allah, the Exalted, were saying: "We brought their journeys near to them," and they said, in arrogance and insolence: "Our journeys have indeed been made distant from us." This reading is also reported from Ibn 'Abbas. Abu Hatim preferred this reading and said: "They did not ask for distance; they only sought something nearer than that nearness, out of insolence and wonder, together with their disbelief."

The reading of Yahya ibn Ya'mar, 'Isa ibn 'Umar, and one narrated from Ibn 'Abbas is "Rabbana ba''id bayna asfarina," with tashdid on the 'ayn and without an alif. Ibn 'Abbas explained it, saying: "They complained that their Lord had made the distances between their journeys far apart."

The reading of Sa'id ibn Abi al-Hasan, brother of al-Hasan al-Basri, is "Rabbana ba''id bayna asfarina." "Rabbana" is a vocative construction; then they stated afterward: "Ba'uda baynu asfarina" (the distance between our journeys has become great), with "bayn" in the nominative by the verb, meaning: "what lies between our journeys has become distant." Al-Farra' and Abu Ishaq transmitted a sixth reading similar to the one before it, with a damma on the 'ayn, except that you put "bayna" in the accusative as an adverb of place (zarf). Its grammatical implication is: "Our travel has become distant among our journeys."

Al-Nahhas said: When these readings differ in meaning, it is not permissible to say that one of them is better than the other, just as this is not said of individual reports (akhbar al-ahad) when their meanings differ. Rather, it is reported about them that they asked their Lord to make the distances between their journeys far apart, out of insolence and arrogance, and it is reported about them that when this was done to them, they spoke of it and complained, as Ibn 'Abbas said.

﴿And they wronged themselves﴾, that is, by their disbelief, ﴿so We made them into legends﴾, that is, people whose stories are told. Its grammatical implication is: "possessors of tales" (dhawi ahadith).

﴿And We tore them completely apart﴾, that is, when what befell them befell them, they scattered and were torn apart. Al-Sha'bi said: "The Ansar went to Yathrib (Madina), Ghassan to al-Sham, al-Asd to 'Uman, and Khuza'a to Tihama. The Arabs used to make them a proverb, saying: 'They were scattered like the hands of Saba' and the arms of Saba'', meaning: the ways and paths of Saba'."

﴿Indeed, in that are signs for every steadfast, grateful person﴾. "Sabbar" is one who is patient in refraining from sins; it is an intensive form of sabir, and one is praised by this name. If you mean that he was patient in refraining from disobedience, the word used for it is only "sabbar 'an kadha" (patient in refraining from such-and-such). "Shakur" means grateful for His blessings. This meaning has already been discussed in al-Baqarah.[[See vol. 1, pp. 371 and 397.]]

The commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 34, verse 20:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And Iblis certainly confirmed his assumption about them﴾. In it there are four readings (qira'at). Abu Ja'far, Shayba, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir, and it is related from Mujahid, read: "wa-laqad saddaqa 'alayhim" with light (takhfif) stress, "Iblisu" with the nominative, and "zannahu" with the accusative, meaning "in his assumption." Al-Zajjaj said: It is in the manner of the verbal noun (masdar), meaning he was truthful toward them in an assumption that he assumed, since he was truthful in his assumption, so it is in the accusative as a verbal noun or as an adverbial of time (zarf). Abu 'Ali said: "zannahu" is in the accusative because it is the direct object, meaning the assumption that he assumed was confirmed when he said: ﴿I will surely sit in wait for them on Your straight path﴾ [al-A'raf: 16], and he said: ﴿I will surely mislead them all﴾ [al-Hijr: 39]. It is also permissible to make the verb "sadaqa" transitive to the direct object, and it is said: "sadaqa al-hadith," meaning "in the speech." Ibn 'Abbas, Yahya ibn Wathhab, al-A'mash, 'Asim, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read: "saddaqa" with the emphatic (tashdid) and "zannahu" with the accusative, by the verb falling upon it. Mujahid said: He assumed an assumption, and it happened as he assumed, so he confirmed his assumption. Ja'far ibn Muhammad and Abu al-Hajhaj [as in the manuscripts of the original and in the book I'rab al-Quran of al-Nahhas; in Ruh al-Ma'ani and al-Bahr al-Muhit it is "Abu al-Jahjaʼ"] read: "saddaqa 'alayhim" with light stress, "Iblisa" with the accusative, and "zannuhu" with the nominative. Abu Hatim said: I see no basis for this reading, and God knows best. Al-Farra' permitted this reading, and al-Zajjaj mentioned it and made the assumption (al-zann) the subject of "saddaqa," with "Iblisa" as the direct object. The meaning is that Iblis beautified for him his assumption about them, something, so his assumption was confirmed, as if he said: "And certainly the assumption of Iblis was confirmed about them." And "ʿalā" is connected to "saddaqa," as you say: "I was truthful toward you in what I assumed about you," and it is not connected to "al-zann," because it is impossible for any part of the relative clause to precede the relative (mawsul). The fourth reading: "wa-laqad saddaqa 'alayhim Iblisu zannahu," with "Iblisu" and "al-zannu" in the nominative, with the light stress on "saddaqa," where "zannahu" is a substitute (badal) for "Iblisu," which is a substitution of inclusion (badal al-ishtimal). Then it was said: This refers to the people of Saba', meaning they disbelieved, altered and changed after they had been Muslims, except for a group of them who believed in their messengers. It was also said: This is general, meaning Iblis confirmed his assumption about all people except those who obeyed God, Exalted is He, as Mujahid said. Al-Hasan said: When Adam, peace be upon him, was sent down from the Garden with Hawwa', and Iblis descended, Iblis said: As for the fact that I have obtained from the two parents what I have obtained, the offspring are weaker and weaker! So that was an assumption from Iblis, and God, Exalted is He, revealed: "And Iblis certainly confirmed his assumption about them." Ibn 'Abbas said: Iblis said: I was created from fire, and Adam was created from clay, and fire burns everything: ﴿I will surely seize his descendants, except a few﴾ [al-Isra': 62], so he confirmed his assumption about them. Zayd ibn Aslam said: Iblis said: O Lord, have You seen these whom You honored, ennobled and preferred over me? You will not find most of them grateful, an assumption from him, so Iblis confirmed his assumption about them. Al-Kalbi said: He assumed that if he led them astray they would answer him, and if he misled them they would obey him, so his assumption was confirmed. ﴿So they followed him﴾. Al-Hasan said: He did not strike them with a whip or a staff; he only assumed an assumption, and it was as he assumed, by his whispering.

(﴿Except a group of the believers﴾) It is put in the accusative as an exception (istithna'), and in it there are two opinions. The first is that it refers to some of the believers, because many believers commit sins and submit to Iblis in some disobedience. That is, among the believers also, only a group was spared, and it is the one meant by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, My servants, you have no authority over them﴾ [al-Hijr: 42]. As for Ibn 'Abbas, it is related from him that he said: They are all the believers, so "min" in this case is for specification (li-l-tabyin), not for partition (li-l-tab'id). If it is asked: How did Iblis know the truth of his assumption while he does not know the unseen? It is answered: When what was executed for him against Adam was executed, his assumption was overwhelmingly that the same would be executed for him against his offspring, and his assumption came true. Another answer is what was answered from His saying: ﴿And incite whom you can among them with your voice, and attack them with your cavalry and your infantry﴾ [al-Isra': 64]. He was given power and capacity, so he assumed that he would control them all by that. When he saw that He accepted Adam's repentance, and that he would have offspring who would follow him to the Garden, and He said: ﴿Indeed, My servants, you have no authority over them, except those who follow you of the deviators﴾ [al-Hijr: 42], he knew that he had followers and that Adam had followers, so he assumed that his followers would be more numerous than Adam's followers, because of the authority of desires placed in his hands, and desires were placed in the bodies of the children of Adam. So it came out as he assumed, when he blew into them, adorned those desires in their eyes, and extended them toward those desires with wishes and deceptions, so the assumption he assumed was confirmed about them. And God knows best.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 34, verse 21:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And he had no authority over them﴾, meaning: Iblis did not compel them to disbelief; he only called them and adorned it for them. Sultan (authority) means power. It is also said it means proof, i.e., he had no proof by which he could lead them astray; they followed him out of desire, imitation (taqlid) and the caprice of the soul, not on the basis of any proof or evidence.

(﴿Except that We might know who believes in the Hereafter﴾) He means the knowledge of witnessing (ʿilm al-shahadah), by which reward and punishment occur. As for the unseen (al-ghayb), He, blessed and exalted, has known it. The view of al-Farra' is that the meaning is: "except that We might know that among you," just as He said: ﴿Where are My partners?﴾ [al-Nahl: 27], meaning according to your claim and in your estimation. His saying "except that We might know" is not, outwardly, the answer to "he had no authority over them"; rather it is to be understood according to meaning, i.e., "We did not give him authority except that We might know," so the exception is disjunctive (munqati'), meaning: he has no authority over them, but We tested them with his whispering so that We might know, and so "illa" here means "but" (lakin). It is also said the exception is connected (muttasil), i.e., he had no authority over them, except that We gave him power over them so that the test might be fulfilled. It is also said that "kana" is superfluous, i.e., "and he had no authority over them," like His saying: ﴿You are the best nation﴾ [Al 'Imran: 110], meaning: you are the best nation. It is also said: when a part of this was connected to the story of Saba', He said: "and Iblis had no authority over those disbelievers." It is also said: "and he had no authority over them in Our previous decree." It is also said: "except that We might know" means "except that We might manifest," and it is like when you say: fire burns wood, and another says: no, wood burns fire, and the first says: come, let us test the fire and the wood so that we may know which of them burns the other, i.e., so that we may manifest that, even though it is already known to them. It is also said: "except that you might know." It is also said: i.e., so that Our friends and the angels may know, like His saying: ﴿Indeed, the penalty of those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 33], meaning: those who wage war against the friends of Allah and His Messenger. It is also said: i.e., so that He may distinguish, like His saying: ﴿that Allah may distinguish the wicked from the good﴾ [al-Anfal: 37]; this meaning has already passed in al-Baqarah and elsewhere. al-Zuhri recited "illa li-yu'lama" in the passive voice.

(﴿And your Lord is Guardian over all things﴾) i.e., He is knowing of everything. It is also said: He preserves everything done by the servant until He recompenses him for it.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Say: Call upon those you claimed besides Allah﴾. That is: this which has been mentioned before, concerning the affair of Dawud and Sulayman and the story of Saba', is among the signs of My power. So say, O Muhammad, to these polytheists: Do your partners have any power over any part of that?

This is a rebuke (tawbikh), and it contains an implied elision: that is, call upon those whom you claimed to be gods besides Allah, so that they may benefit you or ward off from you what Allah the Blessed and Exalted has decreed against you. For they do not possess that. And ﴿They do not possess an atom's weight in the heavens or on the earth, and they have no share in either of them, and He has no helper among them﴾. That is: Allah has no helper among them in creating anything. Rather, Allah alone is the One who brings things into existence, so He is the One who is worshipped, and the worship of other than Him is impossible.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 34, verse 23:**

His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿And intercession will not benefit﴾, i.e., the intercession of the angels and others.

(with Him), i.e., with Allah.

(except for him whom He permits). The common reading is *ádhina* with a fatha on the hamza, since Allah the Exalted is mentioned first. Abu 'Amr, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read *udhina* with a damma on the hamza, in the passive form (*ma lam yusamma fa'iluh*, "the passive whose agent is not named"). The one who permits is Allah the Exalted. The pronoun *man* (in "him whom") may refer to the intercessors, and it may also refer to those for whom intercession is made.

(until, when fear is removed from their hearts). Ibn 'Abbas said: the fear is cleared away from their hearts. Qutrub said: what is in them of fear is removed. Mujahid said: the veil is uncovered from their hearts on the Day of Resurrection. The meaning is that intercession does not come from any of those who are worshipped besides Allah, whether angels, prophets or idols. Rather, Allah the Exalted permits the prophets and angels to intercede, while they are in the utmost fear of Allah, as He said: ﴿And they stand in awe of Him﴾ [al-Anbiya': 28]. [See vol. 11, p. 281.] The meaning is: when they are permitted to intercede and Allah's speech reaches them, they are struck with fear, because of the awesome matter that accompanies that state and their dread that some shortcoming may occur in carrying out what they were permitted to do. When the fear is lifted from them, they say to the angels above them, who are the ones who convey the revelation to them with the permission: (What has your Lord said?), i.e., what has Allah commanded? They reply to them: (They say, "The truth"), which is that He has permitted you to intercede for the believers.

(And He is the Most High, the Great), so He may judge His servants as He wills. It is possible that this permission refers to the worldly life, regarding the intercession of certain peoples, and it is possible that it refers to the Hereafter. There is an ellipsis in the speech, meaning: intercession with Him does not benefit except for the one permitted, who is then startled by what reaches him of the permission, out of reverence for the speech of Allah the Exalted. When the fear is removed from their hearts, he responds with submission. It has also been said: this fear occurs today among the angels with regard to every command that the Lord the Exalted issues, meaning that intercession benefits only from those angels who are today fearful and obedient to Allah the Exalted, unlike the inanimate objects and the devils.

In the Sahih of al-Tirmidhi, from Abu Hurairah, on the authority of the Prophet (ﷺ): "When Allah decrees a matter in the heaven, the angels strike their wings in submission to His word, like a chain upon smooth rock [al-safwan: the smooth stone]. When fear is removed from their hearts, they say, 'What has your Lord said?' They say, 'The truth, and He is the Most High, the Great.' And the devils are above one another." He said: this is a hasan sahih hadith. And al-Nawwas ibn Sam'an said: the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "When Allah wishes to reveal a command, He speaks the revelation. The heavens are seized by a tremor or a violent shaking, out of fear of Allah the Exalted. When the inhabitants of the heavens hear that, they swoon and fall down prostrate before Allah the Exalted. The first to raise his head is Jibril, and Allah speaks to him and tells him from His revelation what He wills. Then Jibril passes by the angels, and whenever he passes a heaven, its angels ask him, 'What has our Lord said, O Jibril?' Jibril says, 'He said the truth, and He is the Most High, the Great.' They all say what Jibril said, and Jibril carries the revelation to where Allah has commanded him."

Al-Bayhaqi also mentioned from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding the words of Allah the Exalted: "until, when fear is removed from their hearts", that he said: each tribe of the jinn had a place in the heaven from which they listened to the revelation. When the revelation descended, a sound was heard like the dragging of a chain over smooth rock. Whenever it descended upon the people of a heaven, they swooned. When fear was removed from their hearts, they said, "What has your Lord said?" They said, "The truth, and He is the Most High, the Great." Then He says, "It will be such-and-such a year, and such-and-such will happen." The jinn would hear this and inform the soothsayers (*kahana*), and the soothsayers would inform the people, saying, "It will be such-and-such a year," and they would find it to be so. When Allah sent Muhammad (ﷺ), they were driven back by shooting stars. So when the Arabs, after the jinn no longer informed them of this, said: "The one in the heaven has perished," the owner of camels began slaughtering a camel every day, the owner of cattle slaughtered a cow every day, and the owner of sheep slaughtered a sheep every day, until they hastened to exhaust their wealth. Then Thaqif, who were the most intelligent of the Arabs, said: "O people! Hold on to your wealth, for the one in the heaven has not died, and this is not a scattering of stars. Do you not see your landmarks among the stars as they are, and the sun, the moon, the night and the day?" Then Iblis said: "Something has happened on earth today. Bring me soil from every land." They brought it to him, and he began to smell it. When he smelled the soil of Makkah, he said: "From here the event has come." So they listened, and behold, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had been sent.

This meaning has already been mentioned in an abridged form, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), in Surah al-Hijr [see vol. 10, p. 10]. The discussion of their being struck with shooting stars and burned by them also appears here, and the explanation will come in Surah al-Jinn [see vol. 19, p. 10 onward], if Allah the Exalted wills.

It has also been said: they are only frightened by the coming of the Hour. Al-Kalbi and Ka'b said: between 'Isa and Muhammad, peace be upon them both, there was a gap (*fatrah*) of five hundred and fifty years during which no messengers came. When Allah sent Muhammad (ﷺ), He spoke to Jibril about the message. When the angels heard the speech, they thought the Hour had come, so they swooned at what they heard. When Jibril descended, he began passing by every heaven, and fear was lifted from them. They raised their heads and said to one another, "What has your Lord said?" They did not know what He had said, but they said, "He said the truth, and He is the Most High, the Great." That is because Muhammad, peace be upon him, is among the signs of the Hour in the view of the inhabitants of the heavens.

Al-Dahhak said: the angels who follow one another (*al-mu'aqqibat*), who come and go among the people of the earth and record their deeds, are sent by the Lord, blessed and exalted. When they descend, a loud sound is heard from them, and those who are beneath the angels suppose it to be a matter of the Hour, so they fall down prostrate and swoon until they know that it is not a matter of the Hour.

This is a warning from Allah the Exalted and an information that the angels, despite their chosenness and high rank, cannot intercede for anyone until they are permitted. When they are permitted and hear it, they swoon. Such is their condition. How then could idols intercede, or how could you hope for intercession when you do not acknowledge the Resurrection?

Al-Hasan, Ibn Zayd and Mujahid said: (until, when fear is removed from the hearts of the polytheists). Al-Hasan, Mujahid and Ibn Zayd said: this refers to the Hereafter, at the coming of death, as an establishment of proof against them. The angels say to them: "What did your Lord say in the world?" They say: "The truth, and He is the Most High, the Great." They acknowledge it at a time when acknowledgment will not benefit them, meaning that they say: "He said the truth."

The common reading is *fuzziʿa 'an qulubihim* (with the verb in the passive). Ibn 'Abbas read *fazzaʿa 'an qulubihim* in the active form (*musamma al-fa'il*, "the active whose agent is named"), with its subject a pronoun referring to the name of Allah the Exalted. As for the one who reads it in the passive, the prepositional phrase (*al-jar wa al-majrur*) is in the position of the subject (*raf'*), and the verb in meaning belongs to Allah, blessed and exalted. The meaning in both readings is: the fear was removed from their hearts, as explained above. A similar usage is *ashkaahu*, meaning "he removed from him what he complained of." Al-Hasan read *fuzi'a* like the common reading, except that he lightened the *zay*. The prepositional phrase is also in the position of the subject, and it is like your saying: "He turned away from such-and-such to such-and-such" (*insarafa 'an kadha ila kadha*).

Likewise the meaning of *furigha* with a *ra'* and a *ghayn* (dotted), lightened, in the passive form (not naming the agent), has been reported from al-Hasan and Qatadah. It has also been reported from both of them *faraghа* with a *ra'* and a dotted *ghayn* in the active form, and the meaning is: Allah the Exalted emptied their hearts, i.e., removed from them, i.e., emptied them of fear and dread, and the passive construction in this reading returns to this meaning. It is also reported from al-Hasan: *faraga* with shaddah (doubled letter).

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Say: "Who provides for you from the heavens and the earth?"﴾ When He had mentioned that their gods do not possess even an atom's weight of what the Lord is able to do, He confirmed this, saying: "Say, O Muhammad, to the polytheists: 'Who provides for you from the heavens and the earth?'" That is, who creates for you these provisions that come from the heavens, namely the rain, the sun, the moon, the stars, and the benefits in them; and "the earth," that is, what comes out of the earth, such as water and plants. In other words, they cannot say, "This is the work of our gods," so they will say, "We do not know." Then say: "Indeed Allah does that, and He is the One who knows what is in your souls." And if they say, "Allah provides for us," then the proof is established that He is the One who deserves to be worshipped.

(﴿And indeed we or you are surely upon guidance or in clear error.﴾) This is said in the manner of fairness in argument, as one says: "One of us is a liar," while he knows that he himself is truthful and his companion is a liar. The meaning is: we and you are not upon one matter; rather, we are upon two opposing matters, and one of the two groups is guided, which is us, while the other is in error, which is you. Thus he denied them in a manner more eloquent than an explicit denial. The meaning is: you are the ones in error when you associate partners with the One who provides for you from the heavens and the earth.

"Aw iyyakum" (or you) is coordinated with the subject of "inna" (indeed). If it were coordinated with the position (of the noun), it would be "aw antum" (or you), and "upon guidance" would apply only to the first party. When you say "aw iyyakum," it is more appropriate for the second party, and the first is omitted; it is also permissible that it applies to the first, and this is the preference of al-Mubarrad. He said: its meaning is that of the words of one who is certain, addressing his companion, to confirm the threat and to rely on clear proof: "One of us is a liar," the meaning being known, as you say: "I do such-and-such, and you do such-and-such, and one of us is wrong," and he knows that he is the one who is wrong. So likewise: "And indeed we or you are surely upon guidance or in clear error."

According to the Basrans, "aw" (or) retains its own meaning and is not for doubt; rather, it is used by the Arabs in such contexts when the speaker does not wish to specify, while knowing the meaning. Abu 'Ubayda and al-Farra' said: it has the meaning of "wa" (and), and its sense is: "And indeed we are upon guidance, and you are in clear error." Jarir said:

Athaʿlabata al-fawaris aw Riyaḥan ... ʿadalta bihim Ṭuhayyata wal-Rababa
[[The version in the Diwan and in Sibawayh's book: (wal-Khashaba).]]

He means: "Athaʿlaba and Riyah." Another said:

Falamma ashtadda amru al-harbi fina ... tamallana Riyahan aw Razaman

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 34, verse 25:

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Say: You will not be questioned about what we committed in sin﴾, meaning, what we earned (iktasabna). ﴿And we will not be questioned about what you do﴾, meaning: I intend by what I call you to only your good, not that the harm of your disbelief reaches me. This is like His saying: ﴿For you is your religion, and for me is my religion﴾ [al-Kafirun: 6]. [[See vol. 20, p. 229.]] And Allah will recompense all of them. This is a verse of truce and disengagement (muhadana wa-mutaraka), and it has been abrogated (mansukha) by the sword (bi-al-sayf). It was also said: this was revealed before the verse of the sword.

Allah's saying: ﴿Say: Our Lord will gather us together, then He will judge between us with truth⦆ — he means the Day of Resurrection. (Then He will open between us with the truth) — i.e., He will judge, rewarding the one who is guided and punishing the one who is astray. (And He is the Opener) — i.e., the Judge with truth — (the All-Knowing) of the states of the creatures. And all of this is abrogated (mansukh) by the verse of the sword.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 34, verse 27:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: Show me those whom you have attached to Him as partners.﴾ Here "arūnī" (show me) may be from the sight of the heart (ru'yat al-qalb), in which case "shurakā'" (partners) is the third object, meaning: inform me of the idols and images that you have made partners with Allah, mighty and majestic is He, and whether they shared in the creation of anything; so explain what it is. Otherwise, why do you worship them? It is also permissible that it be from the sight of the eye (ru'yat al-basar), in which case "shurakā'" is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl).

(Kallā) means: the matter is not as you claim. It has also been said that "kallā" is a rejection of their suppressed answer, as if He said: Show me those whom you have attached to Him as partners. They say: They are the idols. So He says: "Kallā," meaning: He has no partners. (Rather, He is Allah, the Mighty, the Wise.)

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 34, verse 28–30:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We have not sent you except comprehensively to mankind as a bearer of good tidings and a warner﴾. That is, We have not sent you except to mankind, all of them (kaffatan), meaning generally; so there is an inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir) in the wording. Al-Zajjaj said: That is, We have not sent you except as one who gathers mankind together through warning and conveying the message. Al-Kaffah (the comprehensive, all-encompassing) carries the meaning of "the one who gathers." It was also said: its meaning is restraining mankind (kaffan li-l-nas), restraining them from the disbelief they are engaged in and calling them to Islam. The ha' (in kaffah) is for emphasis (li-l-mubalaghah). It was also said: the meaning is "except as one possessing kaffah," so the noun modified has been omitted, meaning one who holds people back from deviating from your conveyance, or one who holds them back from disbelief. From this comes kaff al-thawb (gathering the edge of a garment), because it draws together its two edges.

(Bashiran) That is, with Paradise for those who obey.

(Wa-nadhiran) from the Fire for those who disbelieve.

(But most of mankind do not know) what is with Allah, and they are the polytheists, who at that time were more numerous than the believers.

(And they say, "When is this promise?") meaning your promise to us of the Hour's establishment.

(If you are truthful.) Then Allah, Exalted is He, said: (Say) to them, O Muhammad: (For you is an appointed day from which you will not delay by an hour nor advance) so do not let its postponement deceive you. Al-mi'ad means the appointed time (al-miqat). By this appointed day is meant the time of resurrection; and it was said: the time of the arrival of death, that is, before the Day of Resurrection there is a specific time for you in which you will die, and then you will know the reality of what I say. It was also said: by this day he meant the Day of Badr, because that day was the appointed time of their punishment in this world by the judgment of Allah, Exalted is He.

The grammarians permitted "mi'adu yawmin" with "mi'ad" as the subject (mubtada'), "yawm" as an apposition (badal) to it, and the predicate being "lakum." They also permitted "mi'adan yauman" to be a adverbial of time (zarf), with the ha' in "anhu" referring back to "yawm." "Mi'ada yawma la tasta'khirun" is not valid without tanwin; and the idafah of "yawm" to what follows, if the ha' is taken to refer to the day, would be the idafah of a thing to itself, because of the ha' in the clause. It is permissible, however, for the ha' to refer to the appointment (al-mi'ad) and not to the day.

And those who disbelieved said: it means the disbelievers of Quraysh.

Then Allah, blessed and exalted is He, informed about their condition concerning what awaits them, saying: (And if you could see, O Muhammad, when the wrongdoers are made to stand before their Lord,) that is, detained at the place of reckoning, exchanging words among themselves with blame and reproach, after having been close friends and allies in the world. The answer to "law" (if/if only) is omitted, meaning: you would see a terrible and dreadful matter.

Then He mentioned what they said to one another, saying: (Those who were oppressed will say) in the world, from among the disbelievers, (to those who were arrogant) and they are the leaders and chiefs, (Had it not been for you, we would have been believers.) That is: you led us astray and misguided us.

The eloquent usage is "lawla antum" (had it not been for you). Some Arabs say "lawlakum", which Sibawayh reported. In that case, "lawla" governs the pronoun in the genitive case, and the following noun is nominative as a subject (mubtada'), with its predicate omitted. Muhammad ibn Yazid said: "lawlakum" is not permissible, because the pronoun follows the noun, and since the noun is unanimously nominative, the pronoun must also be nominative.

(The arrogant will say to those who were oppressed: Did we turn you away from guidance?) This is an interrogative with the sense of denial, meaning: we did not turn you away from guidance, nor did we compel you.

(After it had come to you? Rather, you were criminals.) That is: you were polytheists persisting in disbelief.

(And those who were oppressed will say to those who were arrogant: Rather, it was the scheming of the night and the day.) The original sense of "makr" in the speech of the Arabs is cunning and deception; one says "makara bihi, yamkuru", and he is "makir" and "makkar". Al-Akhfash said: it is in the sense of "this is the scheming of the night and the day". Al-Nahhas said: the meaning, Allah knows best, is: "Rather, your scheming by night and day," that is, your private conversations with us and your calling us to disbelief led us to this. Sufyan al-Thawri said: "Rather, your deeds by night and day." Qatada said: "Rather, your scheming by night and day turned us away." The scheming is attributed to the night and the day because it occurs within them. This is like His saying: ﴿Indeed, the term of Allah, when it comes, is not delayed﴾ [Nuh: 4], where He attributed the term to Himself, and then said: ﴿So when their term comes, they cannot delay by an hour﴾ [al-A'raf: 34], since the term belongs to them. This is of the same kind as your saying: "its night is standing and its day is fasting." Al-Mubarrad said: that is, "Rather, the night and the day were your scheming," just as the Arabs say: "its day is fasting and its night is standing." He recited a verse of Jarir:

You blamed us, O Umm Ghaylan, for travelling at night,
Yet you slept, while the night of the mounts was not asleep.

And Sibawayh recited:

So my night slept, and my worry was revealed.

That is, I slept during it. A parallel is His saying: ﴿and the day giving sight﴾ [Yunus: 67]. Qatada recited "bal makrun al-layla wa al-nahar" with tanwin on "makrun" and the accusative on "al-layla wa al-nahar", the implied sense being: "Rather, a scheme exists in the night and the day," and the verb was omitted. It is also permissible for it to be nominative by a hidden verb indicated by "anahnu saddannakum" (did we turn you away), as if, when they said to them, "Did we turn you away from guidance?", they replied, "Rather, the scheming of the night and the day turned us away." It is reported from Sa'id ibn Jubayr regarding "bal makru al-layli wa al-nahar" that he said: the night and the day passed over them and they became heedless. Rashid recited "bal makra al-layli wa al-nahar" with the accusative, as one says: "I saw him as the arrival of the pilgrim," and this is only permissible with what is definite. (When you used to command us to disbelieve in Allah and set up rivals to Him.) That is, equals, likenesses and peers. Muhammad ibn Yazid said: "fulan nidd fulan" means "so-and-so is the equal of so-and-so", that is, his like. It is also said "nadid". He recited:

Whatever you set up as rivals against me,
And you are not, for one of noble lineage, an equal.

This has already been discussed in al-Baqarah.

(And they concealed their regret.) That is, they displayed it. It is one of the words with opposite meanings (addad), meaning both concealing and revealing. Imru' al-Qays said:

I passed through guards and the terrors of a company
Hostile to me, eager, were they to conceal my slaying.

[This is the reading of the verse in the original manuscripts and the Diwan. In al-Mu'allaqat it reads: "I passed guards toward her, and a company / hostile to me, eager, were they to display my slaying." "Yashurun" with the shin dotted means: they display.]

It is also reported as "yashurun". It was also said: (and they concealed their regret) means the regret became evident in the secret expressions of their faces. It was said: regret does not appear; it is in the heart, and only what proceeds from it appears, as its explanation was given earlier in the surah of Yunus and Al 'Imran. It was also said: their display of regret was their saying: ﴿So if only we had a return, we would be among the believers﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 102]. It was also said: they concealed their regret among themselves and did not voice it aloud, as He said: ﴿And they concealed their private conversation﴾ [al-Anbiya': 3].

And they said: "We have more wealth and children." That is, we have been favored over you with wealth and children, and if your Lord were not pleased with what we are upon of religion and merit, He would not have bestowed this upon us.

("And we are not going to be punished.")

Because whoever is shown kindness will not be punished. So God refuted their statement and what they argued with regard to wealth, and said to His Prophet ﷺ: ("Say: Indeed my Lord extends provision to whom He wills") meaning He expands it, ("and restricts it") meaning He constricts it. That is, God is the One who distinguishes among His servants in provision as a trial for them, so nothing of that indicates what their outcomes will be. Abundance of provision in this world does not indicate the happiness of the Hereafter, so do not think that your wealth and children will avail you anything tomorrow.

("But most people do not know.") This is because they do not reflect. Then He said, emphasizing: ("Neither your wealth nor your children are that which will bring you near to Us in position.") Mujahid said: That is, nearness. Zulfah means qurbah (nearness). Al-Akhfash said: That is, izlaf, which is the verbal noun (ism al-masdar), so the place of qurba is in the accusative, as if he had said: "by that which brings you near to Us, bringing near." Al-Farra' claimed that "alladhi" (in the singular feminine form, "allati") applies to both wealth and children together. He also had another view, which is the position of Abu Ishaq al-Zajjaj: the meaning is "Your wealth is not that which brings you near to Us, nor is your children that which brings you near to Us in position," then the predicate of the first was omitted because the second indicates it. Al-Farra' recited:

"We are content with what we have, and you with what you have, though our opinions differ."

Outside the Qur'an it is permissible to say: bi-al-latayn, wa-bi-al-latee, wa-bi-al-lawati, wa-bi-al-ladhayn, and bi-al-ladhina, specifically for children. That is, wealth does not increase you in rank and degree with Us, and does not bring you near in nearness.

("Except one who believes and does righteous deeds.") Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: The meaning is: except one who believes and does righteous deeds, for his wealth and his children will not harm him in this world. Layth related from Tawus that he used to say: "O God, grant me faith and action, and keep me away from wealth and children, for I heard in what You revealed: 'Neither your wealth nor your children are that which will bring you near to Us in position, except one who believes and does righteous deeds.'" I say: Tawus's statement is open to examination, and the meaning, God knows best, is: keep me away from wealth and children that are rebellious, or those in which there is no good. As for righteous wealth and a righteous child for a righteous man, then that is excellent! This has already been discussed in "Al 'Imran," "Maryam," and "al-Furqan." [See vol. 4 p. 72.]

"Man" (the relative pronoun) is in the accusative position as a disjunctive exception (istithna' munqati'), meaning: "but whoever believes and does righteous deeds, his faith and his deeds will bring him near to Me." Al-Zajjaj claimed that it is in the accusative position by way of exception, as a substitute (badal) for the kaf and mim in "tuqarribukum" (which brings you near). Al-Nahhas said: This view is an error, because the kaf and mim refer to the addressee, so substitution is not permissible; if this were permitted, one could say "I saw you Zayd." This statement of Abu Ishaq is the statement of al-Farra'. Except that al-Farra' does not say "badal," because it is not from the terminology of the Kufans, but his statement ultimately leads to that. He claimed that a similar example, ("except one who comes to God with a sound heart") [See vol. 11 p. 80], is in the accusative according to him by "yanfa'u" (benefits). Al-Farra' also permitted that "man" be in the nominative position, meaning: "it is none but one who believes..." Thus he said, but I do not grasp its meaning.

("Those will have the recompense of double for what they did.") That is, the statement: ﴿Whoever comes with a good deed will have ten times its like﴾ [See vol. 7 p. 150] [al-An'am: 160]. So "al-dif" (double) means increase, that is, for them is the recompense of multiplication. It is an instance of the verbal noun being annexed to its object. It was also said: for them is the recompense of multiples, so "al-di'f" has the sense of the plural, and the annexation of "al-di'f" to "al-jaza'" is like annexing a thing to itself, as in "haqq al-yaqin" and "salat al-ula," meaning: for them is the multiplied recompense, for one is ten up to whatever amount God wills of increase. ("And they will be secure in the upper chambers.") The common recitation is "jaza'u al-di'f" with the annexation. Al-Zuhri, Ya'qub, and Nasr ibn 'Asim read "jaza'an" with tanwin in the accusative, and "al-di'fu" in the nominative, meaning: "Then for them is the double as recompense," by way of inversion (taqdim and ta'khir). The majority also read "fi al-ghurufat" in the plural, which is the preference of Abu 'Ubayd, because of His saying: ﴿We will surely settle them in the Garden in lofty chambers (ghuraf)﴾ [See vol. 13 p. 82] [al-'Ankabut: 58]. Al-A'mash, Yahya ibn Wathhab, Hamzah, and Khalaf read "fi al-ghurfah" in the singular, because of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Those will be rewarded with the chamber (al-ghurfah)﴾ [al-Furqan: 75] [See vol. 3 pp. 1141 and 359]. "Al-ghurfah" may be used to mean a collective noun and a generic noun. Ibn 'Abbas said: They are chambers of ruby, emerald, and pearl. The explanation of this has already passed [See vol. 8 p. 204, vol. 13 p. 83, and p. 359].

("Secure") That is, from punishment, death, illnesses, and sorrows.

("And those who strive against Our signs") to nullify Our proofs, Our argument, and Our Book.

("Seeking to frustrate") [meaning] opposing, thinking that they can escape Us by themselves.

("Those will be brought forth into punishment") That is, in Hell, where the guards (zabaniyah) will bring them forth.

al-Qurtubi's commentary (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 34, verse 39:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Say: Indeed, my Lord extends provision to whomever He wills of His servants and restricts it for him﴾. He repeated it for emphasis.

(And whatever you spend of anything, He will replace it) That is: say, O Muhammad, to those who are deceived by wealth and children: indeed Allah expands provision for whomever He wills and restricts it for whomever He wills. So do not be deceived by wealth and children; rather, spend them in obedience to Allah, for whatever you spend in obedience to Allah, He will replace it. There is an ellipsis here, meaning: He will replace it for you. It is said: akhlafa lahu and akhlafa 'alayhi, meaning He gives you its replacement (khalaf) and its substitute (badal). That replacement is either in this world or in the Hereafter. In Sahih Muslim, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "There is no day on which the servants rise in the morning except that two angels descend, and one of them says: 'O Allah, give the one who spends a replacement, and give the one who withholds a loss.'" Also in it, from Abu Hurayrah, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who said: "Allah said to me: Spend, and I will spend upon you..." (the hadith).

This is an indication of a replacement in this world equal to what was spent, when the spending is in obedience to Allah. The replacement may not come in this world, in which case it is like supplication, as mentioned earlier (see vol. 3, p. 308 onward), in terms of being answered, expiating sins, or being stored up; and storing up here is like it in reward.

Question: al-Daraqutni and Abu Ahmad ibn 'Adi related from 'Abd al-Hamid al-Hilali, from Muhammad ibn al-Munkadir, from Jabir, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Every act of kindness is charity. Whatever a man spends on himself and his family is recorded for him as charity. Whatever a man protects his honour with is charity. Whatever a man spends as expenditure, Allah is responsible for its replacement, except what is spent on construction or in disobedience." 'Abd al-Hamid said: I said to Ibn al-Munkadir: "What protects a man's honour?" He said: "He gives to the poet and to the one with a sharp tongue." 'Abd al-Hamid was deemed trustworthy by Ibn Ma'in.

I say: As for what is spent in disobedience, there is no disagreement that it is not rewarded and has no replacement. As for construction, what is necessary for a person to shelter and protect himself is replaced for him and rewarded for its building, and likewise what preserves his body and covers his nakedness. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The son of Adam has no right in anything other than these qualities: a house he lives in, a garment that covers his nakedness, and dry bread and water." This meaning has been fully discussed in "al-A'raf" (see vol. 7, p. 239).

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And He is the best of providers﴾. Since it is said of a person that he provides for his dependants, and a ruler provides for his soldiers, He said: "And He is the best of providers." Created providers do provide, but that is from wealth owned over them, which then runs out, whereas Allah, may He be exalted, provides from treasuries that do not perish and are not exhausted. Whoever brings something from non-existence into existence is the true Provider, as He said: ﴿Indeed, Allah is the Provider, the Possessor of strength, the Firm﴾ [adh-Dhariyat: 58] (see vol. 17, p. 55).

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 34, verse 40–41:

His saying, the Exalted: (And [remember] the Day when He will gather them all together [[The reading "nahshuruhum" (We will gather them), with the nun, is the reading of Nafi'.]]) This is connected to His saying: ﴿And if you could see when the wrongdoers are made to stand before their Lord﴾ [[See p. 302 of this part.]] [Saba: 31]. That is, if you could see them in this state, you would see a dreadful matter. The address is to the Prophet ﷺ, and what is meant is he and his community. Then he said: And if you could also see them on the day "when He will gather them all together," the worshippers and the worshipped, that is, We will assemble them for the reckoning, (then He will say [[The reading "nahshuruhum, naqulu" (We will gather them, and We will say), with the nun, is the reading of Nafi'.]] to the angels: "Was it you whom these used to worship?"). Sa'id narrated from Qatadah: this is a question, like the saying of the Mighty and Majestic to Jesus: ﴿Did you say to the people, "Take me and my mother as two gods besides Allah?"﴾ [[See vol. 6, p. 374.]] [al-Ma'idah: 116]. Al-Nahhas said: the meaning is that when the angels, upon them be the blessings of Allah, deny them, this is a rebuke for them, so it is a question of reproach to the worshippers.

(They will say: "Glory be to You") That is, exalted are You above having partners.

(You are our Guardian, not them) That is, You are our Lord, whom we take as our protector, obey, worship, and sincerely devote our worship to.

(Rather, they used to worship the jinn) That is, they used to obey Iblis and his helpers. In the tafsir books it is mentioned that a tribe called Banu Mulayh from Khuza'ah used to worship the jinn, claiming that the jinn appeared to them, that they were angels, and that they were the daughters of Allah. This is His saying: ﴿And they have made between Him and the jinn a kinship﴾ [[See vol. 15, p. 134.]] [al-Saffat: 158].
