His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when Our clear verses are recited to them﴾ means the Qur'an.

(They say, "This is not but a man") meaning Muhammad (ﷺ).

(who wants to turn you away from what your fathers used to worship) i.e., your forefathers' gods that they used to worship.

(And they say, "This is not but a fabricated lie") meaning the Qur'an, i.e., it is nothing but invented falsehood.

(And those who disbelieve say of the truth when it has come to them, "This is not but obvious magic") At one time they said "magic," and at another time they said "lie." It is possible that some of them said "magic" and others said "lie."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 34, verse 44–45:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Nor did We give them books which they could study﴾, meaning: they did not read in any book given to them that what you have brought is false, nor did they hear it from a messenger sent to them, as He said: ﴿Or did We give them a book before this, so that they hold fast to it?﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 21][[See vol. 16, p. 74]]. So there is no ground for their denial to rely upon, nor any doubtful claim to cling to, as the People of the Book say, though they are in error: "We are a people of a Scripture and of laws, and we rely upon messengers from among the messengers of God." Then He threatened them for their denial with His true words: (And those before them denied) meaning: peoples before them denied, who were stronger than these in might, and greater in wealth, children and ease of life, so We destroyed them, like Thamud and 'Ad.

(And they have not attained one-tenth) meaning: the people of Makkah have not attained (ma'shar ma atayna-hum), i.e. the former nations. The *mi'shar* (ma'shar) and the *'ushr* (ushr) are the same, two dialects. It has been said: the *mi'shar* is the tenth of the tenth. Al-Jawhari said: the *mi'shar* of a thing is its tenth, and they do not say this of anything other than the tenth. He also said: those before them did not attain the *mi'shar* of the thanks for what We gave them; this is related by al-Naqqash. It has also been said: God, exalted is He, did not give those before them a *mi'shar* of what He gave them of knowledge, clarity, proof and evidence. Ibn 'Abbas said: there is no nation more knowledgeable than his nation, and no book clearer than his book. It has also been said: the *mi'shar* is the tenth of the *'ashir*, and the *'ashir* is the tenth of the tenth, so it is one part in a thousand. Al-Mawardi said: and this is the most apparent, because what is meant by it is exaggeration in diminishment.

(So they denied My messengers, and how was My rejection?) meaning: My punishment upon the nations. Within it there is an elision, and its estimate is: "So We destroyed them, and how was My rejection?"

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 34, verse 44–45:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Nor did We give them books which they could study﴾, meaning: they did not read in any book given to them that what you have brought is false, nor did they hear it from a messenger sent to them, as He said: ﴿Or did We give them a book before this, so that they hold fast to it?﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 21][[See vol. 16, p. 74]]. So there is no ground for their denial to rely upon, nor any doubtful claim to cling to, as the People of the Book say, though they are in error: "We are a people of a Scripture and of laws, and we rely upon messengers from among the messengers of God." Then He threatened them for their denial with His true words: (And those before them denied) meaning: peoples before them denied, who were stronger than these in might, and greater in wealth, children and ease of life, so We destroyed them, like Thamud and 'Ad.

(And they have not attained one-tenth) meaning: the people of Makkah have not attained (ma'shar ma atayna-hum), i.e. the former nations. The *mi'shar* (ma'shar) and the *'ushr* (ushr) are the same, two dialects. It has been said: the *mi'shar* is the tenth of the tenth. Al-Jawhari said: the *mi'shar* of a thing is its tenth, and they do not say this of anything other than the tenth. He also said: those before them did not attain the *mi'shar* of the thanks for what We gave them; this is related by al-Naqqash. It has also been said: God, exalted is He, did not give those before them a *mi'shar* of what He gave them of knowledge, clarity, proof and evidence. Ibn 'Abbas said: there is no nation more knowledgeable than his nation, and no book clearer than his book. It has also been said: the *mi'shar* is the tenth of the *'ashir*, and the *'ashir* is the tenth of the tenth, so it is one part in a thousand. Al-Mawardi said: and this is the most apparent, because what is meant by it is exaggeration in diminishment.

(So they denied My messengers, and how was My rejection?) meaning: My punishment upon the nations. Within it there is an elision, and its estimate is: "So We destroyed them, and how was My rejection?"

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 34, verse 46:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Say, "I only admonish you with one thing"﴾ completes the proof against the polytheists. That is, say to them, O Muhammad: "I only admonish you," meaning I remind you and warn you of the evil outcome of what you are engaged in.

(With one thing) means with one word, comprehensive of all speech, which necessitates the negation of shirk in order to affirm the God (ilah). Mujahid said: it is "There is no god but Allah." This is also the view of Ibn 'Abbas and al-Suddi. Also from Mujahid: "with obedience to Allah." It was said: "with the Qur'an," because it comprises all admonitions. It was also said: its implied meaning is "with one characteristic," which he then explains with His saying: (that you stand up for Allah, in pairs and individually), so "an" (that) is in the genitive position as an apposition (badal) to "wahidah" (one), or in the nominative position by implying a subject, meaning "it is that you stand up." The school of al-Zajjaj holds that it is in the accusative position, in the sense of "li-an taqumu" (so that you may stand). This "standing" means standing in pursuit of the truth, not the standing that is the opposite of sitting. It is like when one says: "So-and-so stood up with such-and-such a matter," meaning for the sake of Allah and seeking nearness to Him. As the Exalted said: ﴿And that you stand up for orphans with justice﴾ [al-Nisa': 127] [[See vol. 5 p. 402]]. "In pairs and individually" means singly and in groups, as said by al-Suddi. It was also said: alone with one's own opinion and consulting others, and this is a transmitted saying. al-Qutabi said: debating with others and reflecting within oneself, and all of these are close in meaning. A fourth possibility is that "in pairs" refers to work by day and "individually" refers to work by night, because in the day one is assisted and at night one is alone; this was said by al-Mawardi. It was also said: he said "in pairs and individually" because the mind (adh-dhihn) is the proof of Allah over His servants, and it is reason ('aql). Those who have the most reason have the greatest share from Allah. When they are individually, the thought is singular; when they are in pairs, the two minds confront each other, and knowledge appears to them both that would have been weaker if they were alone. And Allah knows best.

(Then you reflect: there is no madness in your companion) The pause (waqf) according to Abu Hatim and Ibn al-Anbari is on "then you reflect." It was said: it is not a pause, because the meaning is: then you reflect on whether you have tested him in lying, or you have seen madness in him, or corruption in his conditions, or that he has frequented someone who claims knowledge of magic, or learned tales and read books, or you have known him to be greedy for your wealth, or you are able to oppose him with a single surah. When you recognize his truthfulness through this reflection, then what is the matter with this obstinate opposition?

(He is only a warner to you before a severe punishment.) In Sahih Muslim, from Ibn 'Abbas, he said: When this verse was revealed, ﴿And warn your nearest kinsfolk﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 214] and "your close tribe among them, the sincere ones," [[al-Qastallani said regarding the phrase (and your close tribe among them, the sincere ones): it is the mention of the specific after the general, and it was a Qur'an whose recitation was abrogated.]] the Messenger of Allah ﷺ went out until he climbed al-Safa and called out: "Ya sabahah!" [[The phrase "ya sabahah" is with the ha' sukun, a word said by one seeking help, originally when people shouted for a raid, because they most often raided at dawn, and they called a raid "the day of dawn."]] They said: "Who is this calling out?" They said: "Muhammad." So they gathered around him, and he said: (O sons of so-and-so, O sons of so-and-so, O sons of 'Abd Manaf, O sons of 'Abd al-Muttalib), and they gathered around him, and he said: "Do you see, if I told you that horsemen were coming out from the slope of this mountain, would you believe me?" They said: "We have never tested you in lying." He said: "Then I am a warner to you before a severe punishment." Abu Lahab said: "Ruin to you! Did you gather us only for this?" Then this surah was revealed: "Perish the hands of Abu Lahab, and perish he" [al-Masad: 1] [[See vol. 20 p. 234]]. Thus al-A'mash recited it to the end of the surah.

"His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Say: I have not asked you for any reward﴾, meaning, any wage for conveying the message, ﴿then it is yours﴾, meaning, that wage is yours, if I had asked you for it. ﴿My reward is only with Allah, and He is over all things Witness﴾, meaning, Watcher, Knower, and Present over my deeds and your deeds, nothing is hidden from Him, so He will recompense everyone."

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 34, verse 48:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Say: Indeed, my Lord hurls the truth﴾, i.e., He makes the proof clear and manifests it. Qatadah said: "With the truth" means with the revelation (wahy). And it is also related from him: "The truth" is the Qur'an. Ibn 'Abbas said: i.e., He hurls falsehood with truth, the Knower of the unseen (ʿallam al-ghuyub).

ʿIsa ibn ʿUmar read "ʿallamu al-ghuyub" (the Knower of the unseen) in the nominative, as an apposition (badal), meaning: "Say: Indeed my Lord, the Knower of the unseen, hurls with the truth." This is the view of al-Zajjaj. The nominative (raf') may be explained in two ways: on the basis of the position (al-mawdi'), since the position is one of nominative case, or as an apposition to the subject within "yaqdhifu" (hurls). Al-Nahhas said: In the nominative there are two other possibilities: that it is a predicate following another predicate (khabar baʿda khabar), and that it is by supposing an implied subject (idmar mubtada'). Al-Farra' claimed that the nominative in such a construction is more frequent in the speech of the Arabs when it comes after the predicate of "inna," and a similar example is: ﴿Indeed that is true: the contention of the people of the Fire﴾ [Sad 38:64]. 

It is also read "al-ghuyub" with the three vowel marks. So "al-ghuyub" (with kasra) is like "al-buyut" (the houses).[[The wording of Ruh al-Ma'ani: "... al-ghuyub (with kasra) is like al-buyut." The wording of al-Bahr: "As for the damma, it is the plural of ghayb; as for the kasra, it is likewise, for they found two dammas with a waw too heavy, so they used kasra to match the kasra with the ya', and the damma upon the ya' with the waw. As for the fatha, it is a form of intensification (mif'al lil-mubalagha), like sabur."]] And "al-ghayub" is like "al-sabur," and it is the matter that is hidden and concealed to the utmost degree.

"The saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Say: The truth has come﴾. Sa'id reported from Qatadah: He means the Qur'an. An-Nahhas said: The implied meaning is: "The owner of the truth has come," that is, the Book which contains the proofs and arguments.

(And falsehood neither originates nor restores) Qatadah said: "[Falsehood] is Satan." That is, Satan does not create anyone. (And neither restores) Here "mā" is a negation. It is also permissible for it to be interrogative, meaning "what," so that the sense is: "The truth has come, so what remains for falsehood that it could restore or originate? Nothing of it remains," like His saying: ﴿Do you see any remnant of them?﴾ [al-Haqqah: 8], meaning, "You do not see any."[[See vol. 18, p. 216.]]"

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 34, verse 50:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say, "If I go astray, I only go astray to my own detriment."﴾ This was because the disbelievers said, "You have abandoned the religion of your fathers, so you have gone astray." So He said to him: Say, O Muhammad, "If I have gone astray as you claim, then I only go astray to my own detriment."

The recitation of the common readers is "ḍalaltu" (ضَلَلْتُ) with a fatḥa on the lam. Yahya ibn Wathhab and others read "in ḍilltu" (ضِلِلْتُ) with a kasra on the lam and a fatḥa on the ḍad of "aḍillu" (أَضَلُّ). Al-ḍalal (الضَّلَال) and al-ḍalala (الضَّلَالَة) are the opposite of al-rushd (guidance). It is said: ḍalla (ضَلَّ, with fatḥa on the lam) yaḍillu (أضِلُّ, with kasra on the ḍad), and Allah, exalted is He, said: "Say, 'If I go astray, I only go astray to my own detriment.'" This is the dialect of Najd, and it is the eloquent form. The people of al-ʿĀliyah say "ḍaliltu" (ضَلِلْتُ) with a kasra, "aḍillu" (أَضَلُّ), meaning: the sin of my going astray falls upon my own self.

(And if I am guided, it is by what my Lord reveals to me) of wisdom and clear explanation (indeed He is All-Hearing, Near) i.e., He hears whoever calls upon Him and is near in responding.

It has also been said, regarding the connection of the verse: Say, "Indeed my Lord casts the truth and makes the proof clear." The straying of one who strays does not nullify the proof. Had I gone astray, I would have harmed only myself, not that it would nullify the proof of Allah. And if I am guided, that is the bounty of Allah, since He has made me firm upon the proof. Indeed He is All-Hearing, Near.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 34, verse 51:**

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿If only you could see when they are terrified, but there will be no escape﴾. He mentions the state of the disbelievers at a time when they will be compelled to recognize the truth. The meaning is: If only you could see when they are terrified in this world, at the arrival of death or other forms of Allah's punishment upon them. This meaning is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas. Al-Hasan said: It is their terror in the graves at the Blast. He also said that this terror occurs only when they come out of their graves, and Qatadah said the same. Ibn Mughaffal said: It is when they witness the punishment of Allah on the Day of Resurrection. Al-Suddi said: It is their terror on the Day of Badr, when their necks were struck by the swords of the angels, so they could neither flee nor return to repentance. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: It is the army that will be swallowed up in the desert (al-Bayda'), and one man from among them will remain to inform the people of what befell his companions, and they will be terrified; this is their terror. ﴿But there will be no escape﴾: there will be no deliverance, as Ibn 'Abbas said. Mujahid said: there will be no place of refuge.

﴿And they will be seized from a near place﴾: that is, from the graves. It was also said: from where they were, so they are near to Allah, and they cannot escape Him or elude Him. Ibn 'Abbas said: It was revealed concerning eighty thousand men who will raid the Ka'bah at the end of time to destroy it. As they enter the desert (al-Bayda'), they will be swallowed up, and this is the seizing from a near place. I say: There is a raised (marfu') report from Hudhayfah with this meaning, which I have mentioned in my book al-Tadhkirah. He said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said, and he mentioned a tribulation that will occur between the people of the East and the West: "While they are in that state, al-Sufyani will emerge against them from the dry valley, at the height of that affair, until he descends upon Damascus. He will dispatch two armies: one army to the East, and one army to Medina. The army heading east will march until they settle in the land of Babel, in the cursed city and the wicked place, meaning the city of Baghdad. He said: They will kill more than three thousand people, violate more than one hundred women, and kill three hundred leaders [[Kabsh al-qawm: their chief, lord, protector, and the one they look to.]] from the descendants of al-'Abbas. Then they will turn back toward Syria, and a banner of guidance will come out of Kufa and overtake that army at a distance of two nights [[In the book al-Tadhkirah: "at a distance of two miles."]]. They will kill them, and not one informant will escape from them. They will rescue what was in their hands of captives and spoils. Their second army will descend upon Medina and plunder it for three days and nights. Then they will set out toward Mecca, and when they reach al-Bayda', Allah will send Jibril (peace be upon him), who will say: 'O Jibril, go and destroy them!' He will strike the ground with his foot in one blow, and Allah will swallow them up. This is the meaning of His words: ﴿If only you could see when they are terrified, but there will be no escape, and they will be seized from a near place﴾. None of them will remain except two men, one of whom will be a bearer of good news and the other a bearer of warning, and both are from Juhaynah. This is why the saying came: 'The certain news is with Juhaynah.'"

It was also said: "They will be seized from a near place" means their souls will be taken in their places, so they cannot flee from death. This is according to the view of those who say that this terror occurs at the time of the soul's extraction. It is also possible that this is from the sense of *fazi'a* meaning "to answer," as one says: "fazi'a al-rajul," meaning he answered the one crying for help whom he calls upon when fear descends upon him. From this is the report in which the Prophet (ﷺ) said to the Ansar: "You are few when hope is present, and you are many when fear is present." As for the one who said that it refers to swallowing up or killing in this world, as on the Day of Badr, he said: They were seized in this world before they would be seized in the Hereafter. And the one who said that it is the terror of the Day of Resurrection said: They will be seized from the belly of the earth to its surface. It was also said: "They will be seized from a near place" means from Hell, and they will be cast into it.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 34, verse 52:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they will say, "We believe in it"﴾, meaning the Quran. Mujahid said: "In Allah, mighty and majestic." Al-Hasan said: "In the Resurrection." Qatada said: "In the Messenger ﷺ." (﴿But how can they reach [the faith] from a distant place?﴾) Ibn Abbas and al-Dahhak said: al-tanawush (the reaching) is al-raj'ah (the return), meaning they seek to return to the world so that they may believe, and far is that! From this is the saying of the poet:

He wishes that Mayy would return to him, but there is no way to reach her.

Al-Suddi said: it is al-tawbah (repentance), meaning they sought it when it was far off, because repentance is only accepted in this world. It was also said: al-tanawush is al-tanawul (the taking hold of something). Ibn al-Sikkit said: it is said of a man who reaches out to seize another by his head and beard: "nashahu yanushuhu nawshan." He recited:

So she reaches for the pool, grasping from above, a grasp by which she crosses the wide deserts.

[The verse is by Ghaylan ibn Hurayth. The pronoun in "fa-hiya" refers to the camels. "Tanush al-hawd" means she reaches its water. His saying "min 'ala" means from above; he means that they are high of body and long of neck, and that grasp which reaches is what enables them to cross the deserts. Al-ajwaz is the plural of jawz, meaning the middle.]

That is, she takes the water of the pool from above and drinks a great deal, and by that drinking she crosses deserts without needing other water. He said: from this is al-munawashah in battle, which happens when the two sides draw close. A man who is nawush is one of great strength. And al-tanawush: al-tanawul (the reaching), and al-intiyash is like it. The rajiz said:

She used to seize the neck with a seizing.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And how can they reach [the faith] from a distant place?﴾ He says: how can they reach faith in the Hereafter, when they disbelieved in this world? Abu Amr, al-Kisa'i, al-A'mash and Hamza read: "wa-anna lahum al-tanawush" with hamza. Al-Nahhas said: Abu Ubayda deemed this reading far-fetched, because "al-tana'ush" with hamza means distance, so how would it read: "and how can they have distance from a distant place?" Abu Ja'far said: the reading is permissible and good, and it has two justifications in the Arabic language, and this far-fetched interpretation is not the way to understand it. One of the two justifications is that the original form is unhamzated, then the waw was hamzated because its vowel is weak, and that is common in Arabic speech. And in the Mushaf which the community transmitted from the community: ﴿And when the messengers are gathered at their appointed time (uqqitat)﴾ [al-Mursalat: 11], and the original is "wuqqitat," because it is derived from al-waqt (time). It is also said of the plural of dar: adu'ur. The other justification was mentioned by Abu Ishaq, who said: it is derived from al-nata'ish, which is movement in delay, meaning: from where for them is movement toward what has become distant? It is said: "na'ashtu al-shay'" (I took the thing from afar), and al-na'ish is the slow thing. Al-Jawhari said: al-tanawush (with hamza) is delay and distance. "Na'ashtu al-amr, aʼnas'uhu, na'shan" means I delayed it, so it was delayed. It is said: "fa'alahu na'ishan," meaning late. The poet said:

He wished, too late, that he had obeyed me, but after matters happened, other matters have happened.

Another said:

I sat for a time away from seeking glory for you, and you came too late after the news had passed you by.

Al-Farra' said: hamzating and not hamzating in "al-tanawush" are close in meaning, like: "dimtu al-rajul" and "dha'amtuhu," meaning I blamed the man.

﴿From a distant place﴾, meaning from the Hereafter. Abu Ishaq narrated from al-Tamimi, from Ibn Abbas, who said: "And how can they [reach it]?" He said: the return; they asked for it, but it is not a time for return.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 34, verse 53:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And they had disbelieved in it﴾, i.e., in Allah, mighty and majestic. It is also said: in Muhammad (ﷺ), ﴿from before﴾, meaning in the world.

﴿And they hurl at the unseen﴾. The Arabs say of anyone who speaks about what he has no certainty of [[ḥaqq al-amr yaḥququhu and aḥaqqahu: he had it from certainty.]]: "He hurls and casts at the unseen" (huwa yaqdhifu wa yarjumu bil-ghayb). ﴿From a far place﴾ is given as an illustration for one who casts and does not hit the mark, meaning they hurl at conjecture, saying: "There is no resurrection, no rising, no Paradise and no Fire," casting at guesses, as Qatadah said. It is also said: "they hurl" means they cast about the Qur'an, saying: "Sorcery, poetry and the fables of the ancients." It is also said: about Muhammad (ﷺ), so they say: "Sorcerer, poet, soothsayer, madman." ﴿From a far place﴾ means that Allah has put far from them the possibility of knowing the truthfulness of Muhammad (ﷺ). It is also said: he intended remoteness from the heart, i.e., from a place far from their hearts. Mujahid read "wa yuqdhafuna bil-ghayb" in the passive voice (ghayr musamma al-fa'il), meaning they are cast at with it. It is also said: it is cast to them by whoever misleads and leads them astray.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 34, verse 54:

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And a barrier will be placed between them and what they desire, as was done with their counterparts before; indeed they were in disquieting doubt.﴾ Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And a barrier will be placed between them and what they desire.﴾ It is said: a barrier will be placed between them and deliverance from the punishment. And it is said: a barrier will be placed between them and what they desired in the world of their wealth and their families. The view of Qatadah is that the meaning is that when they saw the punishment, they wished that their repentance would be accepted, that they would obey Allah the Mighty and Majestic and comply with what Allah commanded them, but a barrier was placed between them and that, because that was only possible in the world, and that time had passed. The root is (ḥawl), and the vowel of the waw was transferred to the ḥa', so it became a yā', and then its vowel was dropped because it was heavy. As in ﴿as was done with their counterparts﴾: al-ashyā' is the plural of shī', and shī' is the plural of shī'ah. (min qabl) means: with those of the past generations, the earlier unbelieving centuries. ﴿Indeed they were in doubt﴾ means: concerning the matter of the messengers, the resurrection, Paradise and Hell. It is said: concerning the religion and monotheism, and the meaning is one. (murīb) means: one who is cast into suspicion; it is said: arāba al-rajul, meaning he became one who has doubt, so he is murīb. And whoever says it derives from rayb, which is doubt and accusation, says: one says shakk murīb, as one says ʿajab ʿajīb and sha'r sha'ir, for emphasis.

The surah has ended, and praise belongs to Allah, Lord of the worlds.
